GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:

Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that the sum of $200,000 each year for five consecutive years from the first day of April, 1909, be appropriated and set apart from the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada for the purpose of aiding in the providing of protection, safety and convenience for the public in respect of existing highway crossings of railways at rail level, and that the said sums be placed to the credit of a special account to be known as ' The Railway Grade Crossing fund/ and be applied under authority of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.
Motion agreed to, and House went into committee.

It is due to the committee that I should make a short explanation of the details of the proposed Bill. As the general question was discussed at great length a few days ago, it is not necessary for me to add any argument to convince the members of the committee or the country that a situation does exist that needs some remedy. It is not a situation that can be remedied by any theories. To my mind it is a condition that requires a prac-

tical solution. The crux of the remedy, so far as this House is concerned, is the enlargement of the power of the Railway Commission and a contribution from parliament towards the purpose we have in view. Objection has been raised in one or two quarters to the federal authorities making any contribution for the elimination of the dangers of level crossings, it being contended that all the expense should be borne by the railways and the municipalities. There are conditions under whicn that might be proper, and the board will have full power to adopt that principle where in its judgment those conditions exist. But if we are to get rid of this great danger, even partially, I think we must at once be practical, and with that object I have followed to a certain extent, in the drafting of this measure, the policy adopted in every state of the union which has endeavoured to grapple with the problem. Were we beginning railway construction at the present time, it would not be difficult to frame legislation for giving the Board of Railway Commissioners power to protect level crossings hereafter to be constructed. But in a new country like ours we have been so anxious to have railways constructed that the federal authority has aided them, the provinces have aided them, and the municipalities have aided them, and until recent years we have allowed them to have pretty much their own way in regard sto the protection of the crossings. As a result of our combined lack of scrutiny of the construction of railway crossings, and of the different conditions that have arisen owing to growth of population, increased speed of trains and development of the country, it has become necessary for us to take active steps to undo in a measure what we have done, or, in other words, to adapt our legislation to present conditions. It being a question that is practical, I believe the only practical way for this House to deal with it is to assent to a contribution to assist in the elimination of this evil, and in that view I have introduced the resolution. Now, in short, the Bill proposes that we shall contribute $200,000 a year for five years to a fund to be designated for the purpose I have indicated. We do not propose to give the board power to divide the $200,000 as it pleases, but we propose to restrict the contribution in this way. For no crossing shall there be contributed more than 20 per cent of the cost nor more than $5,000. The board may not draw on this fund at all, but we give it power to do so within these restrictions. The board will have power, as it has now, to apportion the cost between the railway, _ the municipality, other person or corporation and this fund. We say other corporation or person, to provide for the case of a toll road owned by a company or the case of a street railway company. It has been a little difficult to de- I
line the crossing, as it may have one track, two tracks, three tracks, or even four tracks.
Is there a limit as to the municipality as well ?

Not in this Bill. In the United States Act there is a limit to the amount contributed by a municipality, but the conditons are different there from those existing in Canada. Conditnons have arisen in Ontario in connection with large viaduct schemes, to which the municipality contributes a larger portion than it does in other cases. The law is not changed in that respect. We are only passing restrictive legislation with reference to the amount we are to contribute ourselves. As to a crossing, we propose to describe that as a work not including more than from one to four tracks. The reason will be obvious. Some crossings might include at terminals fifteen or twenty tracks, and it would not be fair to have the word ' crossing ' mean more than a certain number of tracks. That number I have placed at four. In order that one municipality may not get all the benefit of this fund in one year by having a large number of crossings, we propose to enact that not more than three crossings in any one municipality in any one year shall be contributed to from this fund.
Another important point is that the contributions I have outlined are to be for crossings that now exist, but I am proposing to place a clause in the Act which will say that crossings, hereafter created by railways yet to be constructed crossing highways, shall be constructed at the expense of the company and without any charge on our fund or on the municipality, thus making a distinction between crossings which already exist and those which are to be brought into existence in the future.
I am making some distinction in the_ case of railways not yet built, as to the priority between the railway and the highway. If the railway is run through a section where there is no highway practically, and it crosses no highway, and is built according to the directions of the Board of Railway Commissioners, it ought not to be in the future, if a highway is constructed across the track, in the same position as if the highway were constructed first. In such a case the hoard can apportion the cost as between the railways and the municipality.
Does the hon. minister mean a highway in law or in fact? Will the Act apply where a highway has been set apart by the survey, but not actually constructed?

I have not given that a great deal of thought, though the other day, in discussing it, I drew attention to the fact that a street might be provided for and not be built. That can be discussed in committee and possibly we might

get over the difficulty, if it be a difficulty, by defining what is meant by a highway.
Another definition determines what we mean by a municipality. We describe it as a city, town, incorporated village, township or parish, in order to guard against the word 'municipality' being constructed as a county by some courts.
These are the main provisions, so far as level crossings are concerned, and it is but fair to sav that in this Bill there are certain other items which it would not be out of place to explain for the moment. In our Act as now existing, some difficulty has arisen as to the issuing of bonds. The same difficulty arose under the old country Act,. and the English Act provides for it. I think they provide for it in the Company's Act, but. I propose to provide for it in this Act as it applies particularly to railway companies. It appears that by a judgment in the British courts, when bonds are pledged as security, say as collateral security, they are at that moment treated as having been issued but just deposited as security. In such a case, they could not be re-issued except as a new issue. In looking over the British Act I find they have remedied that. In several provinces they have done it in the Company's Act. In order to clear up the matter, I propose to introduce a clause to cover that point.
There is a question particularly affecting the people of the west and that is the protection along the lines of railway by means of fire guards. I have had representations made by members from the west and also by the railway companies themselves, regarding the power of the railways to plough furrows in lands not on their line for the purpose of protection against fire. I am providing that they may be allowed to do that under conditions to be prescribed by the Board of Railway Commissioners. There is this difficulty that the railway companies think they ought to have the right to go on other property and be exempt from all liabilities for damages. In some cases that might be proper and in others not, because they might in some cases injure more property than they would protect. I have thought it advisable not to release them from any liabilities under the Act. On the other hand we do not want to impose in perpetuity the liability, and we concluded that the fair way was to provide that the railway companies could, under conditions prescribed by the board, establish these fire guards.
There is another point I want to deal with, of great importance to the railway companies and the people, particularly in sections where railway construction is taking place. On all these points I am open to discussion and conviction. The law, as it now stands, provides that if plans are

filed for the location of a railway, no matter how long a time may elapse between the filing of these plans and the taking over of the property, the value of the property shall remain at the price it was when the plans were filed. Let me illustrate. In . a section of country where a railway is to be constructed or a charter granted, the company may proceed to file plans. The companies have their charters renewed. They may have had their plans filed in a certain locality and ten years may elapse before they proceed to take possession of the land for the right of way. The law intended that the land should not increase in value owing to the expected building of railways. It was intended to protect the railways to that extent. But circumstances often arise in which the land increases in value very rapidly, independent of the railway going there, and it hardly seems fair that a company should have the privilege of tieing up the land or keeping it at this high value ten or twenty years before they intend building the road, while the property all around is increasing in value. I propose to say that two years will be allowed after filing of the plans for the railway to obtain a title. That two years corresponds with the time given the railway companies by this House for the expenditure of 15 per cent of their charter. After two years they have to come back and get their charters renewed. I thought it would be fair to make these periods concurrent. I would ask the committee to place a clause in the Bill saying that the_ price of property shall remain as at the time the plans were filed, provided the company obtains titles to these lands within two years of the filing of these plans. That situation has arisen in some parts of Canada, and I think it is but fair that we should apply the remedy. That is a clause I have inserted in the Bill, and at present I think it need interfere with no person.
Will that clause be retroactive, or will the government take care that existing litigations-for there are such, as mentioned by the minister-are not included in this section?

I have not made provision for that in the clause, but I think we would have to guard against interference with present litigation. I am opposed to interfering with any case now in dispute in the courts. These are the main points in the Bill, which I submit tol the confidence of the House. I think I have gone further than the resolution would warrant me in going, but as they are in the Bill I thought it better to make a full explanation.

With regard to the filing of jjlans, the minister has pointed out very clearly what the object of his proposal is, and it is a very laudable object in my

opinion. But there is another defect in this connection, if I am rightly informed, in reference to the filing of plans along and adjacent to navigable waters and harbours. As I understand it, the railway company makes plans and submits them to the railway board, or the minister, as the case may be. The railway board, or minister, might refuse to ratify the plans. But that is not the practice; the plans, as a rule, are ratified. Because, there seems to be no other course. The law is not elastic enough, it seems to me. The railway board ought to have power to ratify such portions of the plans as they see fit, and, later, if the public interests and the business of the road require it, they could ratify further portions. In that way, some portion of the water fronts and harbours might be conserved to the public; under existing circumstances, the railway company usually manages to get it all. Will the minister please consider that point?
I will.

Would the minister explain how he understands the jurisdiction of the railway board as regards municipalities? Does he understand that the board has power, without any Act on the part of the municipality, to order the municipality to contribute towards, let us say, providing means of protection; or is it only when the municipality initiates the proceedings and so submits itself to. the jurisdiction of the board?

I think it is comparatively clear that the board has jurisdiction to compel a municipality as well as an individual. The decision of the board may be made an order of the court by a very simple process. I do not wish to express a legal opinion, not being a lawyer, but 1 have discussed the matter with the Minister of Justice and several other gentlemen, and the opinion seems to be that, even if we did not, in the first instance, have ample powers, the passing of this portion of the Bill, being incident to the working out of the Act in" detail, would give full authority.
Mr. LEN'NOX. I would like to ask another question. Has the minister conferred in any way with any of the provincial governments with a view to their co-operating in bringing about the desired improvement in our conditions?

I may say that I have done so. It is only within the last few days that I have been able to work this Biil out into the shape in which I now have it. It is a very intricate matter, when you come to get it down on paper. I wrote a brief letter to each of the provincial premiers, outlining what I was doing, and asking for their co-operation. I suggested
to them my own opinion that the provinces might care to contribute something, but that it would be out of place for me to urge that view. But I did suggest that it would help in the working out of the Bill if they would give the municipalities any powers they required in reference to raising money for the purposes indicated, as the provincial authorities control the municipalities. I suggested to them also that if the municipalities through themselves, or in some way through the legislature, would consider the advisability of passing certain by-laws as to the necessity of exercising care in crossing tracks, it might be a benefit. I received a reply from the premier of Ontario expressing sympathy with the movement. I shall hear from him again, as they have not had time to discuss the matter fuller. Other premiers have not had time to reply.

There seems to be a consensus of opinion in favour of legislation in the direction of that introduced by the Minister of Railways. There is one matter which the hon. gentleman has neglected to deal with in his speech:	he
did not tell the number of crossings to be provided for, nor whether the grant of the sum proposed each year for five years would be sufficient to wipe out the dangerous crossings altogether, or whether this would provide for only a moiety. In any case, this is a step in the right direction. The nice question arises, that has been suggested by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) as to the power of this House to compel municipalities to contribute to these crossings. In the past, we have dealt with this matter through the Railway Commisison. Municipalities have applied to the commission to have the railway crossings regulated. It may be said, is has been suggested, that, when the municipalities have been applicants, the commission may have jurisdiction by reason of that fact. But I think we have gone further than that; I think that the railway companies have applied to the Railway Commission asking that municipalities should he required to contribute towards highway crossings and that the commission has dealt with that matter. I have expressed myself pretty clearly as to the jurisdiction of this parliament to legislate on these matters. 1 believe it to be quite clear that, as this parliament has power to grant a railway charter, it has the right to legislate on everything incidental to the carrying on of the railway. Property and civil rights are handed over to the jurisdiction of the provinces. But we go so far as to say that a municipality shall contribute towards a railway crossing. We go so far as to say that the railway

company shall have the right to enter into private property adjacent to the railway and make a fire guard.
If we can do that, we can almost do anything in reference to assuming jurisdiction over civil rights and property. My memory is in the past, to a great extent. I have listened to the opinions of the ablest lawyers, and have consulted them with reference to that very subject. I had occasion to consult Sir John Thompson in reference to that matter, and he was clear that where the parliament of Canada had decided that any subject was incidental to something which they had jurisdiction oyer, parliament could exercise jurisdiction over that subject, and the highest court in Great Britain would not inquire whether it was incidental or not. According to that opinion, I think that our jurisdiction is certain. I think there is no doubt that the minister is proceeding in the right direction, because it is clear, from the debates in the House, and the opinions of the press, and of every one else, that the disgraceful state of affairs in this country regarding level crossings must be put an end to. It is but reasonable that the Dominion government should contribute something towards that end. It is a small amount that the Dominion government are contributing, and it could not be left to a fairer court than the Railway Commission to apnortion the amount between _ the government, the railways and municipalities. I congratulate the minister on the resolution, and on the able advocacy of the legislation bv the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) and others. I consider the legislation to be absolutely in the right direction.
Mr. BLA1N. When the minister was explaining his Bill, I notice he said that the limit of the tracks was four. I have in mind one or two very dangerous crossings where there are five tracks over the highway. Why should not the minister make provision for cases of that kind?

My hon. friend will see that I am helping him. Where there are more than four tracks the federal fund could be drawn upon for practically two crossings instead of one. A situation of that kind could call for an appropriation for two crossings on the same highway. I was limiting the Bill to four tracks, because in some places there might be terminals, and I wanted to get away from the large viaduct schemes. In that case there would be nothing to preclude the commission from drawing on the federal fund an amount to equal two crossings.

The same thought occurred to me when the Minister of Railways was limiting the crossings to only four tracks. I have in mind a particular crossing which has been declared danger-Mr. J. G. HAGGART
ous by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, by the Board of Railway Commissioners and by the Minister of Railways himself. There are six tracks. The Grand Trunk has made a shunting ground across the highwav with six tracks,, one running a distance of 25 or 30 feet beyond the highway, but it is sufficient to make six tracks across the highway. I understood the minister to say that he proposed not only to limit the purpose of this Bill to crossings where there were not more than four tracks, but also to limit the number of cases in each municipality.
In any one year.

I would like to understand from the minister whether, for instance, if the crossing I have referred to was taken in, and a portion of the money was given to that crossing-and I believe we could get a portion of it-would that be the same as three crossings in that particular year for that municipality?-because there are six tracks there.
The idea of the Bill is that, for this purpose, you can call a crossing of four tracks or less one crossing; if you had eight tracks there would be two crossings.

Do we understand then that in case of five tracks, if there were one track more than four, the municipality would get double the amount? Would it be $5,000'for each track? It seems to me that would be an unfair proportion. If there were eight or ten tracks the municipality would only be paid for two crossings.

My hon. frienid has missed the point. I have confined the grant to not more than 20 per cent in any case, because they could not get over that restriction, if they did over the other. The Board of Railway Commissioners will have full power to restrict as they see fit. We are adding a limit over which they cannot go, both as to percentage and as to amount.

There was a point I did not understand. If I understood the minister correctly, he confines the operations of this Act to incorporated municipalities. Now in the newer sections of the west, in northern Ontario, and doubtless in other parts of the country, there are settlements close to railways, but there is no municipal organization. I would like, if possible, that people in these circumstances should have the same privilege, and that the minister should extend the Act to places where the people 'have not organized municipally, but where the crossings are just as dangerous as in cities and towns.

There is nothing in this Act to prevent the Board of Railway Commissioners from dealing with crossings' in unorganized districts as with crossings any-

where else. If there is no municipality, there may be some other power upon which they could draw for a portion of the fund. The object of this Act is to eliminate the danger of any level crossing in Canada. So far as possible I have tried to outline the parties among whom the costs should be apportioned.
Can they draw on this fund in the cases I have mentioned?
I think there will be no question about that.

I understand none of this fund will be used to protect level crossings on government railways. I would ask the minister if it is intended in the near future to take into consideration the level crossings on government railways. He must know that in Nova Scotia, for instance, there are numerous dangerous level crossings that should be protected.

That is a matter which gave me a good deal of thought-how we should proceed in regard to government railways. But back of it all we have to remember that it is the same government and the same treasury, whether the money comes out of this fund or out of some other fund. As the government railways pay no taxes to either the municipalities or provinces, the municipalities, with reference to government railways, occupy a somewhat different position from that which they occupy with reference to private-owned railways. In the estimates of this year my hon. friend will find several amounts devoted to the elimination of level crossings. We propose to do at least as good work on the government railways as we are trying to make private-owned railways do throughout the Dominion of Canada.

I understand the minister to say that the word ' municipality ' as defined in this Bill, will apply to cities, towns and incorporated villages. In the province of New Brunswick we have no townships and we have very few villages that are incorporated. Would the municipality or the county be liable in a case of that kind where there was a crossing running through a village that was not incorporated?
In my explanation I intended to use the word ' parish ' in addition to ' townships.'
You did use it.
Would not that cover your case?
Of course, we have parishes.

I certainly am very much pi eased that we are to have a defined nolicy as to part of this question. I maintain a reasonable respect for the Railway Board,
but I have greater faith in the wisdom of 220 men than in the wisdon of five or six ; and what I have set out for particularly in this matter is that we shall have some kind of general principle upon which the question of the control of railway crossings shall be settled. I notice too with pleasure that the minister has a double limit to the liability which we will incur; first, that we shall not contribute more than 20 per cent and secondly that in any case we shall not gc beyond $5,000 for the protection of any one crossing. I am inclined to think that it will be found that this is a valuable limitation, and that, as well, it will probably be found to be a reasonable amount. But, whilst I am very much pleased that we are to have, in part, a defined policy upon the question of railway crossings, I regret- and I hope it will not continue to be a regret, as I trust the minister will take into consideration the advisability of amending his judgment in that regard-I regret that we have not some limit to the contribution to be made by municipalities, if a contribution is to be made by the municipalities at all. If it is necessary that we should have a limit in the case of the country, with its comparatively large resources, I do submit that it is even more important and necessary that we should have a limit in the case of the country, with its comparatively large resources, I do submit that it is even more important and necessary that we should have a limit beyond which the municipalities .shall not be called upon to contribute. The minister might answer me by saying that there is such a wide range to this question that it is hard to place the limit. I know it is, but the limit might be on a sliding scale of some kind.
On a percentage basis.

On a percentage basis, as is suggested, and I think it, will be found to work out very fairly. I would certainly urge that we have a iimit as regards contributions by municipalities, a definite percentage beyond which they cannot be called upon to contribute unless they desire by consent of the council of the municipality to contribute a larger amount. I notice in the findings of the Railway Board that a good many of the cases are adjusted by agreement between the railway companies and the municipalities and it is probably a very fair and desirable way in some instances. I have in my mind, more particularly, the question of rural municipalities. All the same that there _ should be a limit as to all municipalities. Speak-for the moment as to rural municipalities, I want to say a word or two. I said the other day I was of opinion that rural municipalities should probably not be called upon to contribute at all. Some one was disposed to take me to task and ask: Why 'should city municipalities

pay and why should rural municipalities not pay? I did not exactly say that. In
the first place, I thought, that with the able representatives we have here from the various cities of Canada they would be able to present their view of the matter better than I could as to what should be the measure of responsibility of the cities, but I do feel that there is a distinction to be drawn between rural municipalities and cities in this respect. Whilst a rural municipality is benefited by the railway, a city is practically made by the railway and therefore there should be a very sharp distinction drawn between what should be contributed by a city and what should be contributed by a rural municipality. In many cases, the great trunk lines are running through these municipalities and the majority of their trains contribute nothing to the advantage of the municipalities through which they merely run, but in the case of the large city, every train that passes into it is of advantage to it.
Enough as to that. I desire merely to emphasize the one phase of the matter that I do feel that we will not have this matter settled in a satisfactory way and the country will not accept it as being satisfactory unless we adopt the principle which is in operation in. every state of the union. I believe that in every state of the union where they have laws similar to this there is a definite limit beyond which the municipalities cannot be called upon to contribute, and I think it is more essential to have a limit as regards the municipalities than that we *should have a limit with regard to the government. The government have better means of presenting their views of the matter than any municipality can have in this country. I am not going into details of that. I congratulate the minister most earnestly and candidly upon having brought in this measure. There are a great many details, of course, that I am not sure are in the measure, but it would hardly be expected that the minister would, at one fell swoop, bring us down all the details that we might think desirable in a measure of this kind. I am not at all convinced of the minister's reasoning or of the advisability of his attitude as regards the limit of four tracks as constituting a crossing". The more tracks the more it is a crossing and the more deadly it is. I would not like the railway companies to be put in a position to hamper the people of the country, or in small towns, by putting in an extra switch and then, as a result of this saying: There is an unlimited liability on your part to contribute and if you initiate proceedings you will have to contribute at the rate of two crossings for these five tracks. That would hardly be an end to be desired. I do not think that probably a limit of four tracks is advisable although I am not going to absolutely condemn it at the moment. I Mr. LENNOX.
recognize that whilst it may be said to be two crossings, it does not follow that we will pay two full contributions. I recognize that the Kailway Board will endeavour to judge fairly between parties and will make the contribution proportionate to what the circumstances are.
The municipality would have to contribute towards two crossings, would it not ?

I do not think so. I am assuming that the Railway Board would exercise a sound discretion, and that they would not call upon a municipality to contribute double for five tracks of the contribution for four tracks. I think they would make it proportionate having regard to the total expense. Then, as to three crossings a year, I presume that some provision of that kind is necessary. That is three, I understand for one municipality. That is really necessary in order that some kind of equitable arrangement should be made. We want a good deal of information in reference to this question of new railways and new highways. I take it there can be no distinction drawn between a highway which has been put into actual use, and a highway which was set apart on the original survey and which was. an existing highway in law, though not in fact, before the railway came into possession. Am I right in understanding the minister that this applies to providing money not only for protection by way of gates for example, but for separation of grades by overhead or underground crossings.
The elimination of the danger whatever it is.

To read the resolution you would almost think it was confined to grade crossings; it is not happily worded in that regard. A railway grade crossing has come to mean a crossing at rail level but so long as the minister understands it in the way indicated, it is all right. Does the minister intend that this contribution shall apply indiscriminately, not only to the elimination of grade crossings, but to protection by other means such as gates and other safety devices short of separation of grades ?

I think we are going a little too much into details at this stage. Although the Bill does not say so, I believe the board will take the view that there shall be no draft made on the federal fund for the protection of a crossing by a gate-* that would be a matter between the railways and the municipalities-but for the elimination of the grade crossing itself where the expenditure is large.

I draw a sharp distinction between the elimination of a grade crossing and mere protection at that cross-

ing. While I am ready to admit the justice of the Dominion contributing something for the separation of railway and highway crossings where the expenditure is large.
I do not think we should go to the extent of contributing to protection by gates or bells. If the Bill is confined to the separation of grades 1 am in harmony with the minister. I understand that if a railway is constructed after this date that railway shall be obliged at its own expense to provide the necessary protection, and the railway board and the Railway Department will have the duty of seeing that such crossings are properly protected either by separation of the grades or whatever is necessary. But, although it may seem to be perfectly unnecessary when the railway is built to provide protection, it may subsequently become necessary on account of the increase of population to order protection, and I presume the Bill will be so worded that notwithstanding permission should be given to the railway to build without protection at the time of its original construction, the board will still retain control so as to order the necessary protection at a subsequent date. I pro sume also that the Bill will apply to all the railways which we charter this session. Then it is a matter of considerable importance as to who shall initiate proceedings in the matter of protecting the public. Is it to be left to some individual or to a municipality or to the railway companies which sometimes do initiate proceedings for protection. Or, is it intended that the initiation of proceedings for the elimination of crossings upon existing railways shall be the duty of some body like the railway board on behaxi of the public?
The Bill provides for that.

We are to contribute $200,000 a year for the next five years. 1 do not suppose that is going to be the end of our contribution but that is not important now. Will the board have power to commit us beyond the limit of a year? For instance, take the subway in Toronto which will cost $250,000; will the board have power to make an order regulating how much is to be paid by Canada each year as the work progresses for several years in advance?
No.

It would almost seem to be necessary to have some provision of that kind. Now, I shall refer to a matter which is not perhaps directly connected with the question before the House but which has some bearing on it. Mr. Hays said in his Stratford speech that it would cost $50,000,000 to carry out what has been suggested in parliament in this respect. He
did not define exactly what had been suggested in parliament, but he is reported as saying they had 50,000 crossings on the Grand Trunk. Apparently that is a mistake. I inquired in the Railway Department how many crossings there were on the Grand Trunk and the minister suggested that there were probably 3,000. However, the people are determined to have protection at these crossings _ and the railways might just as well criticise what we are doing in parliament in a fair way. Nobody ever spoke of protecting all the crossings or even a large proportion of the crossings in Canada. We all recognize that a great many of them do not require protection, but there is a percentage which do require protection either by separation of grade or some other device, and it is idle for Mr. Hays or any one else however eminent to talk of it costing an average of $17,000 each for all the crossings in Canada.
I apprehend that there is really a very small proportion of the railway crossings in Canada that require protection, and it will be in the interest of the railway companies, and of everybody who desires to avoid the nationalization of railways, to concur with the people's representatives in meeting the demands of the people fairly in this matter. I see that yesterday or the day before, in the discussion of the Lancaster Bill, one of the railway lawyers repeated the heresy of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways-I used the word heresy advisedly, because I get it from one of his own party papers.
You do not generally take them as an authority.

In this case it is fairly good. To consider whether the people are careless or not is not the way to approach this matter. It is not a question whether an accident results from the people's carelessness or not. We know that people are careless, not only in the matter of railway crossings, but in all the various walks of life; in this and in many other respects we have to protect them against their own indiscretions. In reference to this matter the Toronto 'Star' says;
One heresy that ought to be renounced forever is the notion that the public are hound to look out for the trains at crossings. It would he just as reasonable to say that a man has a right to dig a hole in a highway and demand that travellers shall drive carefully lest they fall into the hole. The highways should be made safe. Railway crossings where there is a great deal of traffic should be so guarded that travellers can drive past without thinking of the trains.
I certainly congratulate the minister on having made an advance in this very important matter, and I wish, as far as I am able, to facilitate the passage of this Act,

amended and improved as it passes through the House.

Just a word in reference to the initiation of proceedings. We have given the Board of Railway Commissioners full power to initiate proceedings themselves. In fact, we expect the board to ascertain from the railways and from their own investigations where the most dangerous crossings are, and to deal with them first; but of course applications made by municipalities or others shall be dealt with as at present. With regard to the number of railways to a crossing, in view of the large terminals in the cities, we have to confine the application to a certain number. I hardly think my hon. friend's reference to my good journalistic friend's remark in the Toronto ' Star ' quite works out. A railway is very necessary, while a hole in the road is not necessary, m the public interest.

I do not know that that is a fair way to put it. A hole in a road is not necessary ; neither is a trap on a railway. The railway is necessary, so is the highway, but a hole in the one or a trap in the other, is not necessary. I am glad that the minister has taken some action in this matter, but I do not fully uiidGrst,and. what the policy of the government is. There is a nrovision of $200,000 a year for five years. I would be inclined to think that under the conditions laid down by the minister, that would not bring about a very large measure of relief. Is it the intention that this grant shall be perpetual? In short, how are we to bring about in this country a condition of things that w'ill secure a very much greater degree of safety of life and property at crossings than we have had in the past? The minister has not given us very much light. Of course, we realize that if the country is once committed to a policy of this kind by a sort of agreement with the railway companies, by an implied agreement -with the municipalities, it may have to be carried out by any goverment that comes into power afterwards. That is the reason I am making a little inquiry as to whether the policy is supposed to continue after the next five years, because I feel a personal interest in that question.
You do not want to commit the next government.

There is another point. I am not quite so clear as my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) with regard to dealing with the municipalities. 1 realize fully the doctrine to which he has alluded, and which might be summed up in this way, that any jurisdiction that is necessarily incidental, for the proper exercise of jurisdiction conferred upon
Mr. LENNOX
this parliament, may be assumed by this parliament, and indeed is possessed by this parliament; but there will be this curious complication in connection with these municipalities. Suppose that the parliament of Canada passes legislation which orders, or which authorizes the Board of Railway Commissioners to order, that any municipality in Canada shall pay a certain proportion in respect of protection at a crossing; you are imposing that order upon a body which has not been brought into existence by this parliament, which this parliament could not bring into existence. The powers of that municipal body are limited by its charter, by the Act which creates it; and you might find this parliament, or the Board of Railway Commissioners under the authority of this parliament, ordering a municipal council to do that which under the terms of the- provincial Act creating it, it has no authority whatever to do. You would therefore be confronted with one of two dilemmas: you would order this municipal body to do that which it has no authority to do, which it could be restrained from attempting to do, or you would be obliged to go further and declare that the parliament of Canada could alter or deal with the constitution or charter of that body and give it powers which it had not possessed before. I would think that question would present very grave difficulty. I realize on the other hand that if any municipal body comes before the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada and makes application for protection at a highway crossing, the board, inasmuch as it has the right under the authority conferred upon it by parliament to refuse that application, would also have the right to grant the application, subject to a condition, and that condition might go so far as to declare that the municipal body itself should bear part of the cost. It would be then for the municipality to obtain the requisite power if it saw fit to avail itself of the decision of the Board of Railway Commissioners in that regard. There is one pther point upon which the minister has not been definite. Suppose the protection to be afforded, under order of the Board of Railway Commissioners, takes the shape of some permanent work, which will be subject to deterioration and need repair from time to time, what is the proposal of the minister in that regard? Is this parliament to continue for all time to come to bear its share in the maintenance of this work or are we to be done with it once for all, when we have paid our share in the first instance? That is a subject which ought to be taken into consideration before the Bill is finally passed.

I desire to make a few remarks upon this very important question of level crossings to which a large part of

the Bill applies. I believe there are far more people killed on the level crossings in the country than on those of the cities or towns, and" I do not think that there is any constituency in which there have been so many persons killed and injured upon level crossings as in the one I have the honour to represent. In my view it is certainly the duty of the government to take active measures to protect those crossings In order to justify what I have just said let me mention a few of the serious accidents which have taken place m my own riding. A few years ago, a farmer was going home from the city of London. He had his two daughters with him in the rig. AVhen they came to a level crossing, he looked in one direction and could see no train, but he could not see very far in the other direction on account of the banK through which the railway was cut He started to cross the track, and just when the horse had reached it, a flyer came along at the rate of sixty miles per hour and upon the down grade. He tried his best to get across in time but failed. The train struck him and killed him, and his two daughters were hurled some distance away and picked up dead. The engineer, m giving his evidence at the coroner's inquest, said that when he saw those people on the track a shudder came over him, and he did his best to slow down, but owing to the short distance

he was about twenty yards away -and the great speed of the train coming on the down grade, he could not accommish much in the way of slowing down, so he closed his eves in order to avoid the horrible sight of what he knew was bound to happen. The crash came and the three persons in the rig were killed immediately. That is not all. At the next three-quarters of a mile is the next crossing. There was a business man-and business men are as a rule pretty watchful-driving over the track. He was struck by a tram and immediately killed. Only three-quarters of a mile further on there is another level crossing, where a farmer, who was going home in the broad daylight, was struck by a train and killed. We had yesterday m -the Senate the argument made that everyone should stop just before coming to a level crossing, but the trouble is the horses -o-et frightened, and the driver is afraid to go on or to stop. In the instance I last mentioned, had the man not stopped at all. he would have saved his life. But as the train came closer, his horse became fright-*ened and ran away and got on the track just in time to kill the man. The next crossing is a bridge. How many do you think were killed there? I am glad to say that there were no lives lost there at all. But there are many other accidents to
which I could allude did I not hesitate to take up the time of the House. It is about time that protection should be given at these crossings. In many cases a bridge would do, but in many others a subway would be required. In others a gate and a man would suffice, and in other places probably an electric bell would have the desired effect. Every place should be considered according to its local character and surroundings. But the great question is: all this costs a great deal of money and who is to meet it? Should the companies meet it themselves or should the country help them? When I take up the year-book of last year, I notice that the country has granted to railways $181,025,000, and in addition 52,000,000 acres of land. One would naturally think that when so much has been given by the people, the railways themselves ought to make their crossings safe. However, these railways have been asked for by the people, and as the hon. the Minister of Railways said the other evening, it would be only right that the people should contribute something to assist in curing this evil. My idea is that the government should withhold the bonuses which are being granted to new railways and apply them to a fund to assist in protecting these crossings.	, .
Then, again, I think the municipalities ought to tax the railways a little more than they do. But the municipalities, in my opinion, ought not to be called upon to pay any portion of this expense. Having had some years experience in a large township council and county council, I know for a fact that the people have enough to do to meet their responsibilities in building bridges, making roads and providing public institutions. All this involves a heavy burden. If the municipalities have to pay any part of the expense in relation to these crossings, it will be like paying three times. They would make their direct contribution as municipalities, then their portion of that paid by the province, and also their portion of'that paid by the Dominion. I hope that, in view of the large undertakings now before the country, the municipalities will be free. I am glad the government is taking this matter in hand. It is a great work, and one that the people want carried out I hope it will be done through the government, not the municipalities, assisting the railways and let this great scheme of making our crossings safe be a national scheme, showing to the world that Canada is determined to protect the lives of her people at her railway crossings.

I would like to take up a short time in making a statement with reference to the Civil Service, in a somewhat general way, with the hope that, when we come to the consideration of the Bill which is to be founded on the resolution laid before the House and passed through the committee not long ago, the points that I desire to raise may be taken into consideration. Our Civil Service in Canada has been, heretofore, [DOT]so divided and distributed, so hidden, as it were in numberless nooks and crannies, not only at Ottawa, but all through the country, that I doubt if any of us have had an adequate idea of its extent and work and, consequently, of its importance. If nothing else were to come out of the discussions we have had than the concentration of the attention of the House and country upon this most important factor of the public work of Canada, a great deal will have been gained. Of course a great deal more will be gained if after the attention of the House and country is directed to such an important part of the machinery of the country's administration, it results in a much improved system and a better operation of that great service branch. First, I would like to make a few preliminary remarks as to what has taken place within the last year in the way of the amalgamation of the Civil Service force. I do not think that any of us probably understood, when the Bill was introduced last year and discussed, how much it meant, what change it would make in the Civil Service as we had been accustomed to consider it and to view it.
Well, what has happened? On the 1st day of September, 1908, in pursuance of that legislation, there was a fusion of two large portions of the Civil Service. The old regular Civil Service amounts in its numbers to 1,228; the effect of the legislation of last year was to add to the regular Civil Service brought under statute and regulations, 1,577 who previously to that time had not belonged to it. That is, the legislation had as its first effect to more than double the regular Civil Service at Ottawa. Now I admit that was surprising to myself; and if at the time we were discussing this Bill we had all had an idea that it meant such a very large change in the stated service, probably we would have approached it with a still greater sense of responsibility and duty than we actually did. Those 1,577 persons added to the regular Civil Service make now 2,891, who will figure in 1909-10 on the pay-roll of Canada to the extent of $3,933,757; or, with the proposed flat increase

which was estimated by the Minister of Agriculture at $347,000, will raise that payroll to $4,280,757. That is a veritable standing army, whose pay-roll creeps pretty closely up to the pay-roll of the whole defensive force of Canada, including the militia and regular troops. Well, that does not end it. It is said that about 4,700 are engaged in the employment of the government of Canada outside and beyond the present inside service in Ottawa; and it is probable that the pay-roll of that 4,700 people very nearly equals the pay-roll of the inside Civil Service as it now exists. That makes an army of 7,600 people, with a pay-roll of something over $8,000,000, a civic army which far overtops in its expenses the payroll of the militia and regular troops of this country. Now, I think, as I said before, that after we have drawn the Civil Service out from these lump votes and these contingencies, and these service votes, from its nooks and crannies, and have displayed them in one solid mass under one regular vote to be taken every year, we will have a better idea and a more adequate view probably of our responsibilities in reference to this great force than we have had heretofore.
Well, what came to pass? At a certain time, owing to pressure from both the outside and the inside Civil Service, the government formed a commission, not the first that has been formed, but formed a commission in 1907 to look into the general conditions of this great service of the country. That commission performed its duties, it brought in its report, and it came to the following conclusions as its main recommendations. It found in that service that there was an increasing and rapidly ascending scale and cost of living; it found that there were very often stationary and almost always insufficient salaries paid; it found everywhere in that service, here and outside, the blight of party patronage; on the whole, it found a service the majority of whose members were fairly efficient, I think, and honest in the discharge of their duties, but which was, from the reasons given by the commission, dispirited, discontented, not to say somewhat hopeless, in reference to their conditions and their future. The commission, after viewing those conditions, made the following recommendations:	That a
system of appointment and promotion, based on merit and efficiency, be introduced; the elimination of party patronage; the enlargement of the scope, and a widening of the horizon of the Civil Service, so as to place within its reach the prizes of the service as well as the lesser positions of the same; an increased remuneration of from 12i to 15 per cent to be given with just discrimination; and in the last place, a superannuation system having in view, not only the betterment of the service, but the cheapening of the ultimate cost of the service. These then were the recommendations that came from the Civil Service Commission, an echo of the recommendations of the previous Civil Service commissions, which, from the time they were first issued in this country, have mainly reported along those lines.
Now the government met that commission in a certain way. In the first place, they divided the service into two parts, and they said: We will take the recommendation of the commission with regard to the basis of the service, in reference to the force at Ottawa, but we will not take it in reference to that portion of the Civil Service which is outside Ottawa. Recollect that the recommendations of the commission, founded on their investigations, showed exactly the same generic conditions all through the service, as regards cost of living, as regards the patronage system, and as regards every other point upon which they touched. But the government were not able, at least at-that time, to do anything with reference to adopting any of the recommendations of the commission outside the Civil Service at Ottawa, to include those which, up to that time, had belonged to the outside Civil Service here at Ottawa. So, having cut in two the service, and decided to do something with reference to one-half of it, they let the other half drift for the time being.
I am not going to follow that now; probably some discussion will take place in the House with reference to that question before we get through with the legislation.
What was done with reference to the service at Ottawa now made into the inside civil service ? The idea of basing the system of the service upon merit and the ascertainment of that merit by examination was approved by the government and embodied in_ the legislation relating to the Civil Service. So that, with reference to the service, from this time forward there should be, according to the spirit of the Act, both appointment and promotion based upon merit and experience, such merit and experience to be ascertained in the way that is constituted under the law. But, the government, after having laid down that basis, did not go as far in the matter of conforming to the principle that they had adopted for the law in the classification which they based upon their legislation. Instead of carrying out the commissioners' recommendation and the spirit of the law as regards its basis in having some discrimination and some distinction made with reference to the service as it stood when it came to the matter of classification, the government adopted what might be called the simple mechanical rule-the man was to be placed in the main according to the salary that he at the time happened to be in the enjoyment of. The ne-er do well, in the enjoyment of a certain salary and in a certain class, stood just as good a chance as the

man who had always done his work and done it well. So, in all the different grades, that was the one lack in carrying out the principle of the Bill with reference to classifications. Then, by a simple clause a certain class under the Act, in the outside service at Ottawa, was brought into the new system' on the same mechanical classification. The salary that the outsider insider was in receipt of fixed his position when he came within the Act. No question as to quality, no question as to time of service, no question of any other sort or any other kind but simply, what is his salary. With that *question answered he goes into his class, no that the 1,577 men and women who were added to the 1,228 already in the service came in and were distributed in the service on this one basis of the salary they at the time happened to enjoy. One might say just here that that was not the best condition upon which to start the new system. In that way there was injected into the system at the very start what the appointment of the commissioners on the basis of the Act was designed to prevent. It was desirable that there should be a distinction made between competence and incompetence, as to length of service and as to efficiency in the carrying out of the service. The question as to how to get at that may have been a difficult one, but it is a difficulty that has been met in other countries and it might have been met in ours. The point I wish to establish is that the government have simply taken the mechanical method of classification, and applied it to all classes of the service without regard to those distinctions and discriminations which the principle of the Act and the appointment of the commissioners are supposed to have in view.
Now, do not, Mr. Speaker, have me understood as saying that amongst the outside insiders who have come in there were not good, efficient men even though they had never passed a qualifying or preliminary examination. There were good men in the outside department, men of merit, men of sterling abilities in the way of carrying out thfeir duties, men of great application and great industry. These have been brought into the service and they will not be a weakness to it but will, on the contrary, be a strength to it. All that I want to emphasize is that the government, for the sake of avoiding the care and labour of making a discriminating classification, chose rather not to have the bother placed upon them, and consequently they adopted the easier method of making it absolutely mechanical or nearly absolutely mechanical. _ Then, with reference to the outside service, that part which has been brought into the regular service, the 1,557 employees; how have they beenj brought into the service, and under what conditions? The system of mechanical classification, as it has Mr. POSTER.
been applied both to the outside and inside service by the government has had a bad effect on the service in this respect. I do not think I go too far in saying that this method which has been employed has strengthened the undignified and mischievous spirit of pull and haul in order that a relative advantage should be got under the new classification and under the new arrangement which has had the effect of rather setting back the more sensitive, the more able, the more high minded employee and of giving an advantage to the man who would assert himself and by political or party, or official favour, pull for a better position than he otherwise would have got. As a result of that there is in the service, from one end of it to the other, a feeling of discontent and injustice which it will take a long while to eradicate and which, if it exists in any service, is not for toe better carrying out of that service, does not tend to make it more effective and better working. With reference to the outside-inside service, what was a fair interpretation, when we enacted in July last that the service was to consist of this outside portion and the regular service, and that the outside portion was to be brought in and distributed on the salaries they had? I appeal to every hon. member of this House if it does not strike him as fair play and square dealing to let these outsiders come in at the salaries they had as contemplated by the legislation, and if it would strike any fair man as being square dealing that just prior to the time that the new Act was to come into force, on September 1, a large number of such employees should be arbitrarily increased in their salaries and thus be given a more favoured position under the new Act after the first day of September?
It does not seem to me that it was playing fair with the Act and the spirit of the Act that ministers should take a certain number of their employees and, in view of the fact that they were to come under the classification of the Civil Service Act on the 1st day of September on the salaries they were then receiving, increase their salaries so that they would get a higher classification than under the Act they would be entitled to. I have not had time to go through the whole of the ministerial operations in this respect, but I have looked into some of the larger departments. When the estimates of the Militia Department were going through the Minister of Militia informed me that of the 47 employes who were transferred from the outside to the inside service on September the 1st. not one had had his salary raised within six months previous to September 1st. And. although in the Post Office Department a large number of officials were transferred from the outside to the inside service on

the first day of September, a return laid on the table by the Postmaster General shows that prior to that date none of these men had had their salaries increased in order to give them a more favoured basis in the classification. I have not been able to analyse very closely the return of the Railway Department, but it would appear that the outside employees of that department came to the inside service on the 1st of September with the same salaries they had been enjoying previously. But the same is not true with regard to other departments. Let us see about the Department of Public Works. There is an order in council from the Public Works Department passed on the 5th of May authorizing the continued employment for one year in the outside service, at the salaries specified of 111 nonprofessionals, thirty draftsmen, thirty-three engineers and architects, making in all 174 officials at an aggregate salary of $202,480. The order in council does not state whether the salaries of these men were increased, and one would think that when a minister brings in a report with reference to 174 officials of this class he should state not only their salaries but whether they were increased or not. However it is not stated in the order in council, and I take it for granted there was no , increase. Starting from that ground, however, we find that as time came closer to the 1st of September the Minister of Public Works on the 6th of August by order in council made the following new appointments: three at $500, $700, and $900 respectively; three at $550, $1,250, and $1,900 respectively; two at $800 and $700 respectively, making 8 new appointees with an aggregate salary of $7,350 all dated back to the 1st of April though the order in council passed on the 6th of August. On that same day the same minister brought down 56 special increases to the outside men. running from $50 to $350 per man, all dated back to the 1st of April, and involving an increased charge of $4,300. Then on the 31st day of August, pretty close to the 1st of September, the same minister comes with an order in council increasing the salaries of 60 officials of the outside service to the amount of $9,150, and making 3 new appointments at $3,400 total salaries. That order in council does not state when it is to take effect or whether it is to be dated back to the 1st of April as the others, but I will assume it is to take effect on the date of the order in council. Now, in all the Minister of Public works made 16 new appointments to the outside service involving $15,827 and made 117 increases involving $13,750, a total of $24,500 added before the 1st day !of 'September to the chosen ones of his outside force. It does not require any very skilful investigation to show how this was done with a view
of getting these officials into the inside service on a higher classification than that intended by the Act. Let me give some instances. I shall not mention names at present, but I find here that on the 6th of August one man got an increase of $200 and on the 31st of August he got an increase of $300 making a total increase of $500.

The evident purpose of that was to put this man up to a salary of $2,100 so that when the first day of September came he would get into the classification which had a salary attached to it running from $2,100 to $2,800. Here is another man who is getting $1,750, an increase of $50, on August 6, and $300 on August 31; the result being to put him on a salary of $2,100, ranging up to $2,800. And so I could go through a long list of increases-$50 and $200, $150 and $100, $50 and $150, $300, $50 and $150, $300 and $100, $100 and $300, $150 and $50, $100 and $200, $100 and $200 repeated over and over again, $100 and $250; the object being to bring the man who was getting $1,250 up to $1,600, so that when September 1 dawned he would find himself aft the minimum of a class in which his salary would run up to $2,100 by annual increases. That does not appear to me to be playing fair, in any of three particulars. It is not playing fair with the outside men themselves. They were within twenty-four hours of coming under a discriminating and able commission, who 'would see their merits, and under whose administration promotions and increases, if merited, were altogether likely; and yet that was not awaited, but the ministerial power was brought into exercise, and the minister and his deputy, out of the large force, made one hundred and seventeen increases and placed his selections by these different accretions of salary, in the new coach, in splendid running form, but left all the others, who did not get the ear of the minister, on the outside, to come in as they were and take their chances in the new organization. Neither do I think it was playing fair with the other departments and their outside services. Here is a minister who says:	My view is that in
spirit and in right I ought not to take advantage of the brief power which I have to increase as I please the salaries of _my outside men, and in that way put them into the new service under improved conditions. These other ministers were pressed to do it, that I well know. They refused the pressure, and their outside men enter the new service handicapped as compared with those of the less discriminating and less conscientious ministers. Neither was it fair to the Civil Service itself; I need not labour that point, and it was not fair to the system itself. It was not fair to those in th&

outside service where the discrimination was made; it was not fair to the members of the Cabinet who played fair with their outside men; it was not fair to the general service itself; and it was not fair to the general principle and spirit of the Act.
Let us come to another minister, and here I find that I have to make a retraction. On the ordinary classification which was handed in, I looked at) the transfers that were made-John Smith, $800, transferred at $800; Timothy Brown, $1,500, transferred at $1,500. I ran my eye over the list of the Minister of Agriculture and I said: Here is a man who has played fair; every man who comes into the new is put at the same salary that he had in the old. And I complimented my hon. friend, and my hon. friend took the compliment-blushed under it somewhat, but took it, and swallowed it down; and then, choking a little, said that there might be one or two instances in which he had necessarily to reward merit, but he plumed himself on the compliment. Mr. Speaker, I beg to retract that, and I am going to state the reasons why I do so. According to a return brought down by the Minister of Agriculture himself, I find that he went out like a good shepherd among his outside force, and gathered in the particular sheep that he wanted, called them by name, herded up 146 of them, and drove them into the increase inclosure-81 with an increase of $50 each, 21 with an increase of $100, 15 with an increase of $150, 19 with an increase of $200, 2 with an increase of $250, five with an increase of $300, 2 with an increase of $350, 3 with an increase of $400,
1 with an increase of $450, 2 with an increase of $500, and 1 with an increase of $600; making increases to the 146 persons amounting to $15,310. And the skill with which these increases land the chosen one on the top of the slide when the toboggan is actually ready to go would be amazing if we had not known the Minister of Agriculture before. These were also made effective on the first day of April, many of them, some on the first day of August; but the increases dated back two months or one month, as is shown in the orders in council. Of these 146 a number were increased in May, but the most of them in two days-on the' 28th and 31st of August respectively. The decisive hour was drawing nigh; there was little time left to make hay while the sun shone, and the Minister of Agriculture went to work and made it. Seven were raised so that they got on at the $2,100 up-going scale, 21 so they got on at the $800 to $1,600 scale, by additions of $50, $100, $150, $200 and $250;	7 were raised to the $2,100

It was the fault of his position, of course, of the times and circumstance^ and not done by design, but here are the facts. This hon. minister has 24 farm hands at $35,400, an average of about $1,200 or $1,300 per man; 10 livestock men at $10,100, or an average salary of over $1,000; three exhibition clerks at $2,500, or $800 average; civil government contingencies, 21 men at $14,500, or $700 average; public health, 3 at $6,450, or $2,100 each. The question I have been trying to solve is by what right or authority did he make, after the votes in parliament had been given, increases to amount to $42,510 when he had only a surplus of $12,830 of the amount which was voted. But he went further, and I think it was a few days before the 1st of September he actually looked about him, in the outside world, and he made 45 new appointments. In the year 1908 he made 116 new appointments, involving salaries of $75,310, and the whole of those 116 appointees of 1908, on the 1st day of September, went into the regular Civil Service with the salaries at which he would have appointed them, ranging from $500 up to $1,200. Again I press the question-1 would if the minister were here-as to whether he ha| contravened the spirit and letter of the Act? The old Act and the new Act are at one in this:	The constitutional requirement, as well as the legal requirement, is that before the increase of the salary is voted the appropriation shall be had. Where were all these appointments and all these increases made from when there was no parliamentary appropriation for that special purpose? The minister tries to fortify himself in part by saying that the Act establishing the department gave the minister himself the right to make appointments out of the general service votes. That is, if he had a vote for lands, he could make as many employees as he liked, and do it by the ministerial fiat alone. That is not in the spirit of the law. That law, it seems to me, refers to temporary assistants, and to temporary assistants alone; and I do not think it gives the minister the right to make what are to all intents and purposes permanent appointments. If the minister knew when he was making these 45 appointments that they were not temporary, that on the 1st day of September every one of those men would be in the Civil Service of this country, and could not be got out of it, he was practically making permanent appointments, doing it without reference to parliament, doing it, as I contend, without a special vote. Now what right has a minister, on the 27th day of August, to vote an increase to an employee and to date it back to the 1st of April, 1908? There is no authority in the Act, either the old or the new Act, so far as I can find. That is not in
accordance with the spirit of the Civil Service in its foundation, either in the old or
in the new. Yet dating back has been done by the Minister of Public Works, and has been done by the Minister of the Interior; I am not so certain as to whether it was done by the Minister of Agriculture or not, but I think in some cases it was.
Now it is instructive to take page 536 of the Unrevised ' Hansard,' and look over these six pages and a half of increases and appointments. I want to read a few of them to show how it is done. Here is a clerk who is receiving $550, what you might call a first appointment, with a low salary, and probably in a low class, compared with other classes. This clerk receiving $550, is given an increase of $250 on the 27th August. What is the purpose? To bring the clerk up to $800 so that, on the 1st day of September, he may come into the class running from $800 to $1,600. Another clerk is receiving $550, on the same day a $250 addition is given, with the very same result, that the clerk is raised to the $800 minimum. Another and still another, receiving $500, and $300 of an increase is added on the 27th day of August, and the clerk is brought up into the $800 to $1,600 schedule. I do not want to weary the House by going through all of these. But here is a set of three, where a $400 increase is given on the 31st day of August in order to raise them to a higher class. Here is a clerk receiving $500, and on August 31 gets $228 added. Here is one who is receiving $550, and on the 27th of August $350 is added, and the clerk is raised to the class running from $900 to $1,200. Another addition of $350, and another addition of $350, to bring a clerk up to $1,600 minimum, running into the class from $1,600 up to $2,100. Here is a list of four all in a row, each of them receiving $700, each of them by $200 increases raised to the class, on the next day, running from $900 to $1,200 in the new schedules. I do not want to weary the House by reading the list, but this is the nature of it, from beginning to end. The purpose, in nine cases out of ten, is evident, it is to boost the recipient so that on the next day he may get into the new arrangement on a favoured basis.

There were 29 who received increases for the avowed purpose on my part of putting them into a class under the new Civil Service Act which they could not otherwise have got into. I say frankly that that was my object in giving the increases to these 29 officers. I will give a few instances to show the reasons which guided me, but I wish to speak first in general terms. When I came to classify my whole department, I did so under an entirely new classification from the old one that was in force before. We had that classification made up in certain divisions and subdivisions, clearly indicating the character of the work expected of the officers, and the salary of these subdivisions yere fixed so that a given class of work, whether done by one individual or another, would be paid for on the same basis.
Now in my outside service, while I have done what I could to give fair treatment, and to arrange my men so that they would be adequately paid for the work they were doing, I had never gone into that matter in the different branches of my department as carefully as I did when we came to bring those people from the outside service into the inside service. And why? Because, when they were in the outside service, if at any time when they were paid out of what I may call lump votes, voted, not for the whole service, if at any time of the year I found that a certain man was not being adequately paid for the work he was doing, if I found that he was showing unusual aptitude, and was more valuable than I had supposed, I could go to my colleagues and ask them to pass an order in council to increase that man's salary. I was not restricted by any statute. The hon. member for North Toronto said on another occasion that I ought to have been restricted by the Auditor General's Eeport, and that I had no right in one year to increase a man's salary when, according to the Auditor General's Eeport, he had been paid a certain salary in another year. I take direct issue with my hon. friend. Lump votes were passed for the purpose of carrying on the service; lump votes did not carry with them details of the salaries, or of the officers who were doing that service; and I venture to assert that I was right in maintaining that I had a fiee hand to give those men such salaries as would best secure the efficient performance of the service they were engaged in. In that way I had a free hand, until the Mr. FISHEE.
1st of September, to pay those men more salary than they were getting, when I had evidence that they were worthy of a higher salary. But after the 1st of September, when these men came into the inside service, they were subject to the same restrictions, the same increases, and the same status in their classes, as the old inside service were, and I would no longer have a free hand. Therefore it was incumbent upon me, in justice to these men, to go over their cases more carefully, and to consult with the heads of my different branches and get their views as to the real qualifications of each individual and the salary that ought to be permanently paid to him, as he was formerly getting a temporary salary. Now let me say this, that of all the increases in this list of mine, some 46 in number-not 146 as the hon. gentleman seemed to imply
