In regard to these men who did get increases, I did it on the recommendation in every case of the heads of branches, who consulted with me and made recommendations. I did not pick out political friends, I did not pick out individuals. Why did I not pick out political friends, even if I had wished to do so? My hon. friend read lists of the men who were appointed to the service, and showed that they were appointed after 1896. That is right. It was after 1896, in nine cases out of ten, and the reason was that before 1896 the then Conservative government had not that care of the agricultural interests of this country which they deserved and required. The old Conservative government was starving the agricultural interests of this country, and were not paying enough to carry on the work which the farmers demanded at the hands of the government, and the hon. member for North Toronto, who was then Finance Minister, was the man chiefly responsible for it. The men employed in the Department of Agriculture were asking for more money, they wanted to expand the work of the department, they wanted to do more for the farmers, but they could not get the money from the then Finance Minister, and consequently the agriculture of Canada was starved, and the Department of Agriculture was a little one-horse affair, while to-day it is doing a work commensurate with the immense and grow-

ing interests of the agricultural industry of Canada.

I assume full responsibility for what my friends did at that time. But my hon. friend is just as accurate in saying I was here and .did that, as he is in a good many other of his statements. My hon. friend was then Finance Minister, he had brought down his estimates, he had tried to get his (estimates through the House, and he knows just as well as I do that all the estimates were refused, because the parliament of that day had not confidence in the men who were bringing them down. The parliament of that day did not want these gentlemen to handle the money of Canada any longer, and they wanted to get a verdict of the people on the conduct of that administration. Therefore parliament held up the government of that day, and did not allow them to carry through their estimates, but forced them to appeal to the country, and the consequence was the great debacle which swamped the Conservative party in the elections of 1896. It was not a refusal to give Prof. Robertson a few thousand dollars, but it was a refusal to let the hon. member for North Toronto handle the finances of Canada for the next five years. Let me tell him that while the farmers of Canada had the fullest confidence in Prof. Robertson, and would be glad to see him get tens of thousands of dollars more than he was able to wring out of the then Finance Minister, the farmers of Canada knew well what they were doing when, in the elections of 1896, they drove him from power, and prevented him from handling the finances of this country any longer. And if to-day the present government is still in power, if the hon. gentleman and his friends are still sitting on the left of the Speaker, it is largely because the people of Canada, last October, were afraid that if they allowed the leader of the Opposition to attain to power the hon. member for North Toronto would .again handle the finances of Canada. Judging from what we know, most men, even among Conservatives in Canada, will say that Canada was right
and they will continue to say that just as long as he is in the position which he now occupies in his party-

I am quite willing to. My hon. friend has himself to thank for the digression. I have told my hon. friend that there were some of these men that I gave increases to in order to put them into their proper classes. I will take a few of the first instances. I cannot over the whole 29, but I will take fair instances. First on the list, there is Mr. W. W. Moore, chief of the market section, who got $200 so as to give him $2,100, thus placing him in the class which goes from $2,100 to $2,800. Mr. Moore is the head of an important subdivision in the Dairy and Cold Storage commissioners' branch. The natural place for a man occupying that position in the department is in that division. He had $1,900 last year. I gave him $200 to bring him up to $2,100 which would give him the position in the classification in which the office that he is exercising was placed. I thought that I was right in doing it. I am quite ready to discuss with anybody Mr. Moore's qualifications and I am going to tell my hon. friend from North Toronto that Mr. Moore was appointed by the Conservative party, was in the department before this government came into office, and was an officer of that Prof. Robertson that I have been talking about. The next is Mr. McNeill. Mr. McNeill is the chief of the fruit section of the Dairy and Cold Storage commissioners' branch. I also gave him $200 to put him in the same subdivision. Mr. Barr is chief of the dairy section or subdivision of my department, and I gave him $300 to put him in the same position. Now I just want to say that Mr. McNeill is so well known amongst the fruit men of this country and so much thought of that I had been asked to make a special branch of my department devoted to the fruit industries of the country, and to put him at the head of that branch. If I had yielded to that Mr. McNeill would not have been in the $2,800 class, but in the $4,000 class. I think I am justified in having given him $200 which will place him in the next division below that to which he might have been advanced. Mr. Barr is a dairy expert, well

known to many hon. members of this House, whose position in the dairy world and in the department as chief of the dairy subdivision requires that he should be put in the division to which he has been advanced. Therefore, he was put up to $2,100 in order to place him in that subdivision. The next I come to is Mrs. Henderson, a clerk. Mrs. Henderson is an old employee. She had been receiving $700. The subdivi sion which she would have gone into would have been subdivision B of the third division. She was such an industrious, painstaking and competent clerk, that the head of the branch in which she is employed recommended that she ought to go into the higher subdivision of the third division, and I gave her $200 to put her at $900. This enabled her to get into that subdivision. The next is a stenographer, Miss Robinson, and she was advanced just in the same way. The next is Mr. Charlan, who is the chief of the tobacco division of my department. This is a gentleman of scientific attainments, whom I was able to secure, a short time ago, from the French government. He was an expert in tobacco growing in the Department of Agriculture of France, and I brought him out to Canada on purpose to help to increase and encourage the tobacco growing industry of this country. Mr. Charlan has made good in an eminent degree and yet, when he first came, he did not know the English language well enough to be of a great deal of use in the English speaking parts of the country. But he has learned the language so well that to-day he is of just as much service in the province of Ontario and in the west as in the French parts of the province of Quebec. He has been placed in the division which begins at $2,100 and goes up to $2,800. At first he was given a tentative salary until we could find out what he was worth to the country and under these circumstances I have given him an increase of $400. I am ready to stand up and justify it from one end of Canada to the other. These are some of the instances that I take at the beginning of the list.
Now, I shall take one or two at the end of about the same character, although, in some cases, the amounts are smaller. There is one which I think my hon. friend mentioned which is a very big one. I gave a gentleman $600 and I did not do it to put him in another division. He got that increase on the 22nd April last and just for this reason: He had been studying veterinary science. He worked for us at $600 a year during his vacation. He was getting $600 last spring. He obtained his degree as a veterinary and then came back and asked me to employ him. Having qualified himself, having got his degree as a professional man, he came back into the Mr. FISHER.
department and I naturally and properly doubled his salary and gave him the same salary that other veterinaries employed in the department had been getting. If I had not done so I would not have done my duty to the department or to Mr. Laidlaw. I have another case, that of Mr. Spencer. Mr. Spencer is in charge of the live stock division. He was paid $1,950. He has charge of one of the most important sub-divisions in my department. I gave him $150 so as to put him in the $2,100-$2,800 class. Mr. Spencer's work, his knowledge, his reputation in the country, amply justify putting him in that class and I would not have been doing that which was due to myself and to the department if I had not done so. These are specimens of those for whom I did this. I do not conceal it and I do not desire to conceal it; on the contrary, I boast of it, because it is a recognition of men who have done good work for the country, of men who are doing good work, of men who ought to be encouraged to do good work and whose positions in tUe department I wished to recognize by placing them in higher subdivisions than they would otherwise have been in. I did that before the first of September for that express purpose and I do not deny it. I repeat that I do not wish to conceal it and that I was only doing my duty by the men, by the work and by the department in doing what I did. These are instances which show that the conclusions reached by my hon. friend from North Toronto are entirely wrong in dealing with the list which I have given him. Instead of his showing me up as one who has taken advantage of the law to do what I had no right to do, I have shown that I was simply carrying out my duty to the men who were in my department, and preparing for the proper exercise of the new law which brought these people into totally new circumstances and new conditions as distinguished from the conditions under which they had been in the old work and under the old regime. My hon. friend says that these men are all Liberals.

The hon. gentleman (Mr, Foster) implies, although he did not say it, that the men who got increases have been nicked out because of political or personal favouritism. Well, in many of these branches the whole staff have been appointed by me personally and I did not give the whole staff increases. Of course I gave them all the statutory increases at the commencement of the fiscal year, but when it came to give the increases when this new Act was to come into force it was my officers at the head of the divisions who picked out the men who seemed to be specially worthy. My hon. friend has complained of discrimination, but he [DOT] has overlooked one point. Supposing we had done as he _wanted and brought these men in at their salaries before the 1st of September, after the 1st of September we either had to give them their statutory increase or promote them to another class. In some instances we gave them enough increase to give them promotion before they came in. In other instances where they were given an increase that did not promote them we would have been tempted to, and probably we would have promoted them after they came m and given them a larger increase because they deserved exceptional recognition. But if the recommendations of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) were carried out and we waited until after the Act came into force and had then gone to the commissioners, the commissioners could only have given tbem a certificate for promotion and they would have had to get that promotion, and that promotion in some cases would have been far greater than the increase they got before they were brought in. The result would have been that the cost to the country would probably have been greater than under the arrangement we made.
My hon. friend speaks about the competence of the old inside service. I myself have stated on a former occasion that m 9 cases out of 10 and probably more the old inside servants were competent and did their duty faithfully. But when they once got in at the bottom of the old inside service they rose step by step simply by _sen-icrity on their statutory increases, without picking out any of the good to put above the less good. The men in the outside service were not in that position. They could be raised without regard to the statutory increase. They could be picked out by the chiefs of their branches and given special increases because they were deserving of them. The men who got this particular favour at my hands before the 1st of September last were so picked out by their own chiefs, and on the recommendation of their chiefs I did what I did. For years back there has been more discrimination and more promotion for merit in the then outside service in Ottawa than there was in the old inside service under the old regime, because the minister and his chiefs had free hands and could do as they thought proper. The men who are at the head of these outside branches of mv department are all of them without exception enthusiasts, earnestly having at heart the work of their branch. They were appointed for that reason; they were appointed as special technical experts; they were picked out of the best men among the agriculturists of Canada, and during the years they have held their positions compliments have been showered upon them by Conservatives as well as by Liberals. They have had the commendation of the Committee of Agriculture of this House over and over again, year in and year out. And these men having at heart the good of the service and wishing to make their branches as perfect as possible were more likely to recommend the good men than to recommend the bad, and to take merit as the sole ground upon which to recommend for promotion. I venture to say, with regard to the increases of the salaries of the outside servants that merit was the only guide. So far as I am personally concerned and I can only speak with _ certainty for myself every one of these increases was given upon the recommendation of the head of the branch, and I know some of these officers ; in nine cases out of ten, I do not

The figures I have I got from the Finance Department, which made out the estimates and gave me the figures a few weeks ago, and there has been no change since. The figures were 2,695 in the whole service. My hon. friend gives 2,800 and something. He says that of these 1,577 came in from the outside. That would leave only about 1,300 of the old inside service. I have not here to-night the information on which I based the statement I made last year, when the Act was going through the House, that there were from 1,500 to 1,600 then in the inside service, and that the probability was that the Act would bring in 800 or 900 from the outside, making the total about 2,500. According to the figures given to me by the Finance Department, that number has been exceeded bv about 200.
, My hon. friend tallied very much about injustice to those who were at the maximum of their class, and who may have to wait for promotion. That has always been the case in the Civil Service, and it must al-ways_ be the case so long as we have a classification. Men who reach the maximum of their class have to stay there until they are promoted. As a general rule, the good clerks, the best clerks, get promoted. Those clerks who are being paid all they are worth, when they get to the top of their class, stay there, and it is just because they are being paid all they are worth that they they do stay there.
My hon. friend seems to think that we have been guilty of a gross and glaring injustice in this respect; but what is the fact? The fact is simply that we have increased the maximum of all the classes, all except one at any rate; so that we gave to the clerks who have been for years at the maximum of their class, an opportunity of going higher and getting an increase to their salaries. Is this an injustice for which we are to be blamed? Have we done this to injure these people? My hon. friend points out that it is chiefly the old clerks, who I suppose were appointed by himself and his friends, who are suffering this so-called injustice. All I can say

is that if any of his friends have remained for any length of time at the maximum of their class, they must have been inferior clerks, and not those who would certainly get promotion if they were very long at the head of their class.
My hon. friend criticises the flat increase.
I do not know that it is right to discuss that on this occasion, because we have a Bill before the House in regard to it. I shall only say that while my hon. friend condemns the flat increase and considers it a very improper method of dealing with the service, the representatives of the service themselves state that they are thoroughly satisfied with it. We did not adopt the flat increase hastily. We recognized that the old Civil Service Commission had recommended a percentage increase, and we tried to work that out on various bases; but we found great difficulties and inequalities in the way. We found that the percentage basis went in a different direction from the sense and spirit of the recommendation of the commissioners, which was that those in the lower ranks of the service should get a greater increase than those in the higher ranks with large salaries. Under these circumstances we believed that by giving a flat increase of a certain amount, a larger percentage of increase would go to those whose salaries were low than to those whose salaries were high; and this was recognized last year in the representations made to the government. In the discussion of the question before the commission; and otherwise, it was pointed out that it was the middle and lower ranks of the service that needed the increase more than those receiving high salaries ranging from $3,000 to $5,000 a year. Under these circumstances we decided to give the flat increase. There is a Civil Service Association in Ottawa which is thoroughly representative of the service, over 90 per cent of the whole inside Civil Service belonging to it. That association chose a delegation to go to the Prime Minister and discuss this question of an increase of salary. They made several propositions, which we discussed and tried to work out ; and eventually in a final interview between that delegation and myself, to whom the matter had been turned over by the Prime Minister, as I was in charge of the Bill, we made the proposition of a flat increase, and after the delegation duly nominated for that purpose by the Civil Service Association, had taken the time to discuss and think over the proposition, they agreed to it without hesitation, and gave me authority to use their personal names, if I chose, as evidence of their agreement. But they went further than that. As a tesult of that agreement the Civil Service Association, composed of over 90 per cent of the whole force in Ottawa, discussed 'the question at a meeting of its executive committee, and passed a
resolution endorsing the action of the subcommittee which had conferred with the government regarding the reorganization of the service and the proposed general increase. Here is a paragraph from a letter addressed to myself from the secretary of the association:
I have also to state that a cordial vote of thanks to yourself for your action on the matter was unanimously passed by the executive at the same meeting, and that I am instructed to convey the same to you, together with an expression of the appreciation of the sub-committee for the kind manner in which you received its representations.

The date of the letter is January 27, 1909 and of the resolution January 21. I may say this-and I have no doubt it is partially the inspiration of what we have heard to-day from the hon. gentleman, that an anonymous communication, typewritten, was sent to me and many others complaining of the flat rate, but evidently whoever wrote this anonymous communication had not the pluck to sign it. I have here a letter from the secretary of the Civil service Association in which he says :
Mr. McGiverin has just written to me with
regard to an anonymous statement which he and several members of parliament have received in which complaint is made of a feature of the proposed increase and he suggests that it might be well to advise you as well as himself in the matter.
The statement in question ha9 also been sent anonymously two or three times to the officers of the association. It does not represent in any way the attitude of the association. That attitude remains, as defined to you by our subcommittee and in my letter to you of January 27, which was written after the publication of the resolution.
That letteT is dated March 9. Mr. Coates goes on to speak of the thirty-five who receive no increase either under the reclassification or the new Bill and asking if possible to provide for such cases under the reclassification. I may say that when we came to work out this question of a flat increase, I was agreeably surprised to find that there were only thirty-five in the whole service at Ottawa who got no benefit under that proposition, and also surprised to And that when you take the whole amount paid and the number benefited, the average percentage of increase comes to almost exactly what the Civil Service Commissioners recommended, or about 12 per cent. That is a most extraordinary working out of the recommendations of the Civil Service Commission. Although we proceed on slightly different lines, we get to the same point and same result, and I believe it to be an abundant justification of what we have done and the manner m which we have done it.

I dare say I have omitted some of the many points my hon. friend has taken up, but I think I may safely say that I can just as satisfactorily answer them as I have been able to reply to those of which I took a note. In the work we have done during the last year, we have placed the Civil Service in a much better position than it ever enjoyed before. We have put a large number into the inside service who deserved to be there and who ought to be permanent and get any benefit derived from being in the inside service. Their work in Ottawa was practically the same as the work of those in the inside service, and it was unjust that they should be working side by side, doing similar work, under a different regime. We have given the service a better status, we have given them an improvement in their classification, and we propose to give them a flat increase in salary to rectify the great difference in the cost of living to-day compared with what it was some years ago. In my investigation I found that in 1857 the permanent officers began at $500 just as they did last year, and this is an evidence that a change was required in the system. In doing this for the Civil Service, I believe we have acted in the interests of the country. My hon. friend began by pointing out what a great army of civil servants we have and what a large sum of money is paid them. That is true. And he compared it with the militia and armed forces of Canada. Well, I venture to think that the men on whose honesty and efficiency we .must rely in the transaction of the business of Canada, deserve just as much consideration as those who may happen to take up their rifles and serve their country under arms. I do not [DOT]want to minimize what these do but merely to point out that both are working in the interests of their country. If our public administration is to go on in an efficient and successful manner, it must be conducted by men who are satisfied with their lot, who take a pride in their work, and who are properly and fairly recompensed for the work they are doing. I think I have been able to justify the work I have done in my own department. Of course, we cannot expect sympathy and support from gentlemen opposite, but I am satisfied that we are getting that sympathy and support from the great majority of the people who have sent us to parliament to represent them.

I repeat again that to bring about, at that time and in the manner adopted, these changes in the administration of this department, in the administration of the Public Works Department, in the administration of the Department of the Interior, was unworthy of the hon. gentlemen who preside over those departments; and I commend rather to the approval of this House and of the country the attitude and the action of the other ministers of the Crown, who thought it their duty to leave those matters to the adjudication and the judgment of the Civil Service Commissioners appointed for that purpose. The Minister of Agriculture has admitted the whole case put by my hon. friend from North Toronto this afternoon. I venture to hope that the administration of this Civil Service Act will be carried out in a fair spirit in the future. No Act can be made perfect, no Act can be put upon the statute-book, which will not leave something to the administration of the heads of the departments; and if this Civil Service Act is interpreted, if it is carried out, in the spirit so definitely boasted of by the Minister of Agriculture this evening, then all I can say is that this Act will prove to be of much less benefit to the Civil Service and to the public of Canada than we believed it would be when we passed it last session. Under the circumstances I think my hon. friend from North Toronto was thoroughly justified in bringing this mater to "the attention of the House, and in pointing out very forcibly the abuse which has been perpetrated by the heads of no less than three departments, upon the very eve of the coming into force of so important a statute as this.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).

speechtext: I shall occupy the attention of the House for a few minutes only, because my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture has so thoroughly justified, as it seems to me, the action of his department and that of the Minister of the Interior, based upon the general powers which were given to the departments of the Civil Service Act, that it is scarcely necessary for me to make any further argument in support of what we have done. Now if the leader of the opposition will pardon the suggestion, I think it would have been much better for him to confine his remarks to a discussion of what the various departments have done under the Civil Service Act, rather than to deal with matters relating to the elections of 1896 and subsequently.

speechtext: Let me remind my hon. friend that I did not introduce that question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MEN OF DREDGE ' NORTHUMBERLAND ' AND THE VOTERS' LIST.
speechtext:
Then if he did not introduce it, he went one better than the Minister of Agriculture. However, I suppose my hon. friend is to be pardoned for still entertaining some feelings of discomfort by reason of what took place last October. Now, Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to affirm that in my judgment the departments which were called upon to deal with the men and women who were in the outside service and who, under the statute were to be brought in to the inside service, simply discharged their duty when they fixed the status which these officials should occupy upon coming into the inside service. That, I apprehend, was our duty under the Civil Service Act; and if my hon. friends had intended to raise any objections to the heads of the departments taking that course the time to raise the objection was when the Civil Service Bill was before parliament last session. What, Sir, was our duty? Let me turn to section 8 of the Civil Service Act passed last session, and which provides as follows:
1.	As soon as practicable after the coming into force of the Act, the head of each department shall cause the organization of his department to be determined and defined by order in council, due regard being had to the status of each officer or clerk as the case may be.
2.	The order in council shall give the names of the several branches of the department, with the number and character of the offices, clerkships and other positions in each, and the duties, titles and salaries thereafter to pertain thereto.
Now what was I called upon to do as head of my department? I found that I had about 36 officers who came within the provisions of the old Civil Service Act; I rad about 170, or perhaps more, who, although they had been for a long time in the department, performing work just as important, performing work of just as permanent a character as that which they would have performed if they had been within the old Civil Service Act, still remained there as temporary employees, although many of them had been there ten, twenty, twenty-five and thirty years, and had to be appointed year after year, and their salaries to be determined by order in council. Now in organizing my department, in acting under the requirements of section 8 of the Act, surely it was my duty to have regard to the services which those officials were performing. it was my dutv to have regard to the efficiency with which they performed their duties, to the length of their service, to the value of .the service they were giving to the country, to the number of people who were qualified to enter upon the dif-

ferent classes which it was my duty to organize under the Civil Service Act. Well, what did I do? I asked the deputy head of my department to do what the statute says he should do, and that is to take into consideration the number of people who were in the department, the services which they were performing, with a view to asking the Governor in Council to fix their status, and to fix the salaries which would pertain to the positions they would be called upon to fill under the Act. Now, probably I knew even less of my officials than other ministers who had been in charge of their departments for a good many years. I did not know the capabilities of those different officials. I would not have the same knowledge of the value of the services which they are performing, as the deputy head of the department. It is his duty to keep in touch with all the officials of the department, and I asked him to take the matter up, and to devote to the subject the greatest possible care, to see that every official who was being brought in from the outside service, received due recognition, and that in placing him in the one class or the other, a most earnest attempt should be made to do simple justice to him, without doing any injustice to any other official. Not days alone, but weeks and weeks were occupied by the deputy minister in the discharge of that duty. He consulted with the heads of the different branches, and I have reason to believe that he discharged that duty conscientiously, with a sincere desire to carry out the terms of the Act, and to discharge the duties which devolved upon him under the provisions of the Civil Service Act. Now what did we do upon his recommendation? Having regard to the different classes which the Civil Service Act declared should be established, we provided that in sub-division A of the first division there should be a certain number of the higher officials of that class. There would be some who were within the Civil Service Act already, and there would be others who would be brought in under the Act on the 1st of September. We selected those officials who were performing the highest duties in the department, and recommended that they should be placed in sub-division A of the first division.
Let me call upon the hon. member for North Toronto, who says that a grave injustice has been done to the old members of the Civil Service, to those who have been under the old Civil Service Act, to take the classification which was passed in council, and which, upon his own motion, was submitted to parliament,_ to point to a single instance where an injustice had been done to those who were formerly under the old Civil Service Act and who have been placed in subdivision A of the first division in my department. At the best he might perhaps
have been able to make the point that there had been some error and that some injustice had been done, but my hon. friend has not ventured to do that, and I may say that if he attempts to do that he will fail in showing to the House that such has been the case. I have never heard that any one of the gentlemen who have been in my department, those who came under the terms of the old Act, have uttered any complaint as to the mode in which they have been treated by the classification which has been made and by the salaries which are to be paid to the various officials who are classed in subdivision A of the first division. _ Then, we have subdivision B of the first division, and, having regard to the various officials in my department of the outside service as well as the inside service, it was the duty of the deputy minister to consider all these officials, the duties which they were performing, the efficiency with which they were discharging their public duties and, having regard to those who ought to go into that division I, upon his initiation, recommended to council that a certain number of officials should be placed in subdivision B of the first division. That was in order to recognize the merits of a large number of the officials and to place in that subdivision those who we thought would be fairly entitled to be placed there. If you will look over the classification which has been made by the Governor in Council upon my recommendation as the head of the department based, as I have said very largely and almost wholly upon the recommendation of my deputy minister, the permanent head of the department, it will be found that we have provided as best we could and according to our best judgment for these various officials both in the inside and the outside service whom we were called upon to place and to whom it was our duty to give the requisite status pursuant to the classification which was made and which is now before the House. As I have said, if my hon. friend could take that classification, if he could take the different officials who have been appointed to these various offices in my department and show that any wrong has been done, that any injustice has been done to any one of these employees, whether those who had been formerly in the Civil Service or those who had been long in the department, although employed in the temporary organization which was instituted a great many years ago, he would be able to make some point against me in connection with this part of the management of my department, but my hon. friend has utterly failed to do that. I recognize that it was my duty, as I assume the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) recognized that it was his duty, to provide for the classification of the various officials in the department, to specify the number of

officials who would be respectively in the different classes, and I assume that it was his duty as it has been my 'duty to have regard to the various officials then in the department and to the services which they were performing as well as the faithfulness with which they had discharged the duties that they owed to the public. In doing that I endeavoured, and I have no doubt that my deputy endeavoured, to so arrange the classification and to so provide for the placing of the different officials as to do complete justice to the officials having regard to their service, the length of their service and the efficiency with which they were discharging their duties.
Just a word with regard to what I thought was an unfair or undeserved insinuation of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) that there had been some favouritism and that some officials who had been appointed by the previous government had been discriminated against. As fax as my department is concerned I can assure my hon. friend that there is no warrant for making-not the statement-but for throwing out such an insinuation as that which was conveyed in the statement of the hon. gentleman. I find that one of the most important officials of my department, to whom there was an increase of $400, was appointed on the 20th March, 1891, under the government of which my hon. friend was a distinguished member. I find that the next gentleman to whom there was an increase of $650 was appointed on the 2nd of March, 1886, also under the former government. Another one occupying a very important position to whom an increase of $300 was given was appointed on the 13th July, 1882; another one to whom an increase of $200 was given was appointed on the 11th April, 1888; and another one to whom an increase of $200 was given was appointed on the 4th December, 1886. And so, if my hon. friend will take this statement which was brought before the House on his own motion and go over the names of those gentlemen who have received an increase, he will see, I am sure, that he has no warrant for making the suggestion that there has been any discrimination as between officials who have been recently appointed and those who have held office in my department for a great many years.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman give the names of those to whom he has just referred ?

speechtext:
I will be very glad to. There is Mr. Adams who received an increase of $120; he was appointed on the 1st May, 1886; Mr. Chasse, the law clerk, who received an increase of $400, was appointed on the 20th March, 1891 ; Mr. Coleman, clerk in charge of returns, who received an increase of $300, was appointed on the 13th Mr. PUGSLEY.
July, 1882; Mr. Cusson, assistant keeper of the records, who received an increase of $200, was appointed on the 11th .April, 1888; Mr. Delaney, assistant photographer, who received an increase of $250, was appointed on the 4th December, 1886; Mr. Desautels, clerk of attendance book, who received a small increase, was appoined June 22, 1886 ; Mr. Lefleche, registration clerk, who received an increase of $200, was appointed on the 8th September, 1887. These are a few illustrations of the truth of what I have stated. So that they apepar to have received the benefit of the increase entirely irrespective of the dates of their appointments. I am sure that an examination of the return which has been submitted to the House will verify the statement which I unhesitatingly, make that in the increases which were given in my department, in the classification which has been made and in the number of officials who have been respectively assigned to each, there has not been the slightest favouritism and that no one has received any increase by reason of the position he may have occupied politically prior to his becoming connected with the department. I have not allowed, and I do not think that the deputy of my department has allowed, political, or party, or personal considerations to enter into the matter in any way, shape or form. We have simply endeavoured to do justice to all ; we have endeavoured to recognize the merits of the different officials and to treat them as we have felt they ought to be treated, and in doing what we have done I challenge my hon. friend himself to show that we have dene other than what it was our duty to dc under the Civil Service Act.
It was our duty under section 8 of the Act to arrange for the classification of the departments, and in doing that it was also our duty to have in view all the different officials who were in the outside as well as in the inside service, and who under the terms of the law were to be brought within the Act, and to have Tegard to the salaries which they would receive because their salaries as of the first of September would fix their status under the Act. In doing so we simply acted within the powers conferred upon us by the Act. The hon. gentleman asks why we did not leave this for the Civil Service Commissioners to do. Well, the Act gives them no power to do what we have done in justice to these officials. The Act does not give the commissioners the power to arrange the classification ; the Act does not give the commissioners the power to say whether in the first division or in the second division or in any other division there shall be twenty officials or ten officials. That is a duty which rested upon the heads of the departments and upon the Governor in Council. It is a duty we could not relegate to the

Civil Service Commissioners ; we could not ask them to discharge a duty which parliament had imposed upon us. It was our duty to say how many of our clerks and which of our clerks should be placed in a certain class, and having regard to the services which they performed and to the claims which they had, it was our duty to fix their salaries so as to do complete justice as between the outside servants and the officials who were within the Civil Service Act, starting everything as from the first of September and after that leaving the working out of the Act and the matter of promotion and of salaries to the commissioners. We have done our duty; we started them under the Act on the first of September and hereafter it will be1 for the Civil Service Commissioners to perform their duty under the terms of the statute.

I may say that I differ entirely from -the conclusion of the minister, but that it is so absolutely immaterial in view of another clause of the Act that I shall not waste time discussing it. Section 8 is:
As soon as practicable.
Not after the prorogation of parliament, not after July 20, but:
As soon as practicable after the coming into force of this Act.
And when did it come into force. Section 48 says:
This Act shall come into force on the first day of September.
And therefore, it is as soon as practicable after the first day of September. Surely a more monstrous proposition was never addressed to an astonished House than that of the Minister of Public Works who carefully tells us that the ministers in promoting these men and in increasing their salaries, acting like a shah, or a sultan, or a rajah or any other oriental despot, did all that by virtue of the power given them by section 8 of the Civil Service Act which says, that after the first day of September they are to call their deputies together and do so and so. But, the minister tells us that ha did it before the first day of September so as to avoid the very effect which
parliament intended should have been produced had he done as he was bidden by parliament after the first of September.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MEN OF DREDGE ' NORTHUMBERLAND ' AND THE VOTERS' LIST.
speechtext: Will my hon. friend pardon me; I think he misunderstood me.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MEN OF DREDGE ' NORTHUMBERLAND ' AND THE VOTERS' LIST.
speechtext: Oh.

speechtext: Just wait a moment; I did not intend to say and I do not think I. did say that we completed the work of classification until after the first of September. What I did say was that in my department for weeks before that we were preparing and arranging for the classification of the various clerks and then when the law came into force on the first of September, we had the matter arranged as we thought equitable and fairly, and they were placed under the various classes pursuant to the terms of the Act. That is what I intended to say.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MEN OF DREDGE ' NORTHUMBERLAND ' AND THE VOTERS' LIST.
speechtext: [DOT] You were caught that time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MEN OF DREDGE ' NORTHUMBERLAND ' AND THE VOTERS' LIST.
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MEN OF DREDGE ' NORTHUMBERLAND ' AND THE VOTERS' LIST.
speechtext:
If the ministers did what they say they did before the 1st of September, they did not do it in pursuance bf the Civil Service Act, for that Act says they are to do it after the 1st of September. At all events the result of what they did was to bring about a state of affairs that would not have been brought about had they obeyed the Act and did it as soon as practicable after the Act came in to force. We therefore have the extraordinary result that a certain number of favoured individuals had their salaries increased before the 1st of September in qrder that they might get benefits which the law did not contemplate they should get. In my opinion everything so done by the ministers was wholly illegal. Is it not a rather singular ilustration of retributive justice that the gentlemen who began to reform the Civil Service by acting in defiance of the statute should now come down to this House with a further measure of reform to add $150 to the salaries of other civil servants in defiance of another statute of this country. I mean the election law. Has any one in this country the slightest doubt that this resolution granting $150 to the civil servants is the price deliberately paid by the government for the seats of the city of Ottawa? Is there a person in this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific who does not know that the government had dis-paired of carrying Otawa and had to abandon the candidates nominated by a duly qualified party convention? Is it not known from the Atlantic to the Pacific that when even the Prime Minister was brought to Ottawa-and I do not think it was paying much of a compliment to Ottawa in view Of the fact that he would not declare he would sit for Ottawa if elected-despite the 1 appeals made on the ground of the wonder-

ful favours conferred by this government on Ottawa, they found that even he could not be elected for Ottawa in the face of the feeling which existed amongst the civil Servants, until his colleague gave a promise, supported and backed up by the Prime Minister, that if-to use plain ordinary everyday Anglo-Saxon-if Ottawa did the square thing by the Prime Minister they could depend upon it that the Prime Minister would do the square thing for the Civil Service. And so we - see how one wrong step leads to another, and that these hon. gentlemen commenced to carry out this measure (which last year was heralded throughout the land as such a marvellous system of Civil Service reform) by very carefully violating it so as to bring about results that could not be attained if they did not violate the statute, and then to complete their work, they had to bring down this measure to carry out the promises which everybody in Canada knows were relied upon by a large section of the civil servants in Ottawa when they voted for the Prime Minister. While I have a great respect for the Civil Service of Ottawa, while I feel that many a member of it is sadly underpaid, and while I would be willing to go as far as any member of this House in doing justice to the hard-working and worthy members of the service, I feel like voting against this resolution, for two reasons; first, because I think it is an insult to parliament to ask us to carry out that illegal promise made during the last election, and secondly, because I believe it is an insult to the intelligence of parliament to ask us to remedy a wrong, which it is admitted has existed in the Civil Service for years, in so haphazard a fashion as giving an increase of $150 all round, irrespective of the salary now received, the length of service, or the ability shown by the recipient-irrespective of 'everything except the promise made last session to increase the salaries of the Civil Service. Surely there is another apd a better way than that; and if this matter comes to a vote, I for one, will vote against the resolution-first, because I decline to be a party to carrying out that illegal promise, and secondly, because, instead of doing justice to the service, it is making a hodge podge of them, and increasing the salaries of many who should not be in the service at all, but should be turned out on the first opportunity. If this were done and the money thus saved were divided among the rest of the service, we would have a far more useful and efficient service than we have.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who has just taken his seat was probably not in the House earlier in this session, when the matter to which he has referred was brought up by the hon. member for North Mr. NORTHRUP.
Toronto. I refer to the so-called promise that was made during the last election. The statement that was made by me in regard to the increase of salaries to the Civil Service, was simply in accordance with the intention expressed in the House last session by the government of carrying out the recommendations of the Royal Commission appointed to inquire into the Civil Service. The only promise that was made by me was that I would use my best endeavours to have those recommendations carried out.

speechtext: What about the letter?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MEN OF DREDGE ' NORTHUMBERLAND ' AND THE VOTERS' LIST.
speechtext: That is exactly what the letter contained, and no more than that. That letter is in 'Hansard,' and if the hon. gentleman who has interrupted me had taken the trouble to look at it, he would have seen that there was no improper promise of any kind. I do not hesitate to say that the government, in putting through the Civil Service Act of last session, has taken a great step in Civil Service reform, and so far as I am able to judge in the city of Ottawa, the government and the commissioners are carrying out that Act fairly and honestly. There are no appointments being made that are not made in accordance not only with the letter but with the spirit of the Act; and when the hon. gentleman who has just sat down says that the government, in bringing forward a measure to grant the Civil Service a flat increase of $150, is not carrying out their policy of last session, I take issue with him, and will strongly support that measure. It is in no way a bribe, but is simply carrying out what was intended last session, and what, owing to the lateness of the session, it was impossible to carry out then. I had no intention of taking part in this debate, because I understood, from what had been said, that no fault could or would be found with the increase that is proposed; and I for one, knowing that the Civil Service Association are fully in accord with this proposition, give it my most hearty support.
