This item stood at the request of one or two hon. gentlemen who
were desirous of seeing the leases of buildings in Ottawa. Those leases were shown to them, and I would like to have this item considered. I might say, in answer to a remark made by one hon. gentleman, I think the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) that I am quite sure that if he makes

inquiry he will find that the observations he made in regard to the rent being paid to the Imperial Realty Company of Ottawa were entirely without foundation. The hon. gentleman stated that the building was worth something less than $200,000, and that an enormous rent was being paid for it, no doubt to party friends of the government. I have made inquiry, and I find that some time ago bonds were issued on the building to the Royal Trust Company of Canada, and it was valued by valuators chosen by that company at $400,000. As to the building being owned by party friends of the government, I have taken occasion to look into the list of directors of the company, and I find that one is Mr. J. W. Woods, another is Mr. Finnie, manager of the Bank of Ottawa, and another is Mr. E. B. Osier, of Toronto, a gentleman very well known to hon. gentlemen opposite, and a very distinguished member of this House. I am sure that my hon. friend, if he were here, would be the first to withdraw the suggestion he made.
A member stated to me to-day that he had spoken to Mr. Osier and Mr. Osier denied the statement that he is a director of this realty company.
That is my information.
He denies it.

As the hon. gentleman says that Mr. Osier denies that he is a director of the company and as two or three members are absent who would like to say something on the subject, it is only fair to put this item off for another night.

I do not like to refuse my hon. friends when they make a request, but I am sorry we have to put this item off. Of course I accept at once the statement, if Mr. Osier authorized it to be made, that he is not a director. My information is that he is, but no doubt, I am misinformed. However, I am quite willing to take up the Nova Scotia items.
Avonport pier-Repairs, $2,000.

The length is about 65 feet. The wharf became badly dilapidated. This is done by days' labour.
Bad deck wharf improvements, $1,500.

This is to complete the improvements to the wharf and also to level up the land and drain it. The original cost was $14,709.
Mr.. MADDIN. What was the cost of the site and was the work let by tender?
The lot is 107 feet wide bv 306 feet deep. The lot and the wharf, including building, was purchased for $3,000 from Mr. Alex. Macdonald.
Was the work let by tender?
Yes, the contract was let for $11,709.
Will the $1,500 complete the work?
Yes.
What is the balance due on the contract?
This is to finish up the total expense. I do not know whether it is all in the one contract or not.
Would this be for extras?

I find there is some extra work required, such as levelling up and draining. The appropriation last year was $3,500. The crib-work retaining wall is estimated to cost $696; filling in old work, $114; filling in space between warehouse and old work, $42; levelling ground, $111; repairs to the old warehouse, $120; new warehouse, $200; fitting up office, $200; superintendent, $350; due the contractor, $400-making a total of $3,500. That will exhaust the $2,000 used out of last year's vote and the $1,500 we are asking for.
Was the warehouse built by the man who secured the original contract?
No.

I find in the report of the Department of Public Works of 1908 that in addition to the construction of the wharf, an agreement was entered into with the contractor for the construction of two boat landings. May I ask if the contractor for the warehouse also built the two landing stages?
I have no memorandum on that point.	.
I am reading from the report of the engineer contained in the minister's report.
In looking at it, it is evident that the landing stages would be included in the $11,709.23.
So, the landing stages would be an extra. Were they constructed by the contractor who built the wharf?
Yes, I take that to be the case.
Can the minister give me the name of the contractor who built the wharf, or, if not, can he give the name of the man who built the warehouse?
I have not a memorandum on that point.

I feel like asking the minister to furnish the information. I can find in the Auditor General's Report the name of the man who built the wharf and

also the name of the man who built the landing stages, and I would like to know if it is the same contractor who built the warehouse.

I will instruct the deputy minister to get that information, and, later, when we consider the general vote, my hon. friend (Mr. Rhodes) will have an opportunity of discussing it. Will that he satisfactory?
Bay St. Lawrence harbour, $5,800.
How much was spent there last year?
This is under contract. There was expended, up to the 30th December, to the contractor $20,890, and to the inspector $283.75-a total of $21,173.75.
What is the nature of the work?

Providing a safe boat harbour by opening a channel about 360 feet long, with a width of 60 feet at the bottom and a depth of two feet at low water. This is made through the beach which separates the pond from the sea. There is also pier work on either side and protection of the channel on the inside.
What will be the depth of water at high tide?
Nine or ten feet, probably; I think the tide rises there about seven feet.
Does the engineer give it as his opinion that the sand will not fill up the channel?
The belief is that building the protection work will have the effect of preventing the channel filling up.
This does not make a harbour of refuge, as I understand it. I suppose it is only for the fishing fleet that fishes off the north end of Cape Breton?
It is only for small boats, drawing nine or ten feet of water.

It is a large expenditure for that purpose.
Big Bras d'Or wharf-close piling and repairs, $2,000.
Is creosoted timber used there?

Yes. The old piling is destroyed. This is a revote.
Blue Rocks harbour-improvements, $4,009.
This is a revote also. It is to provide funds for the construction of a dam at the eastern end, and a breakwater at the western end of the harbour.
No, by contract given after public advertisement and tender.

Will this amount complete the work?
Mr. PUGSLEY;. This Us expected to complete the work.
Breton Cove-extension of breakwater pier,
This is a work of diversion of the mouth of the stream to the north of the wharf. It is a revote. The work is under contract.
What is it expected to accomplish?
It is to prevent gravel from washing around the end of the wharf and so interfering with the boat landing.
How extensive are these works?
The amount is $5,788. This vote is to pay the balance.
What will the works consist of when completed?
An extension of the present breakwater pier, 120 feet out to deeper water.
I doubt very much whether the work will stand. There is a tremendous sea there.
We hope it will stand; and the engineer thinks it will.
Is creosoted timber used there also?

Yes.
Cheverie breakwater-extension of, $4,500.
When was the contract entered into ?
On the 16th of December, 1908.
How many tenders were received?
Four, ranging from $4,295 to $5,270. There were four tenders between those amounts.
When were the tenders called for ?
About a month previous to that time. It is expected this will finish the work.
What is the extent of the extension ?
Eighty feet.

Is this work being done with creosoted timber.
I do not think this is
Is this being carried on by Mr. PUGSLEY. day's work?	creosoted timber.
What is the policy of the department, and on what principle does it use creosoted timber in some works and not in others ?

Creosoted timber would be used in localities where the worms are found to be very destructive.
Church Point-repairs to wharf, $600.
This is to finish up the work.
Would the minister define what he means by conductor of works and sub-conductor ? I see that both of these titles appear in the Auditor General's Report.
A conductor, my deputy informs me, is one who performs the functions usually performed by a foreman. A sub-conductor would be a labouring man who had an oversight of the work under the foreman.
I see elsewhere in the Auditor General's Report that the terms foreman and subforeman are used in public works. Are these synonymous with conductor and sub-conductor?
I think so.
Is not a conductor merely an inspector, so to speak ?
No, I think a conductor actually works himself.

On this item I would like to refer to the landing pier at Westport, in the county of Digby, with regard to -which I asked the minister a question a few days ago. In the estimates of last year was an item of $3,000 for the purpose of beginning the construction of a public landing at Westport, and the minister informed me that nothing had been done, and it was not intended to go on with the woTk during the present year. Some time later when the matter of these deferred public works generally was under discussion, the minister made a statement of his policy in reply to a question. I will quote from ' Hansard ' page 1348 :

Will the minister also give us the assurance that those public buildings which were in the estimates last year and which now are unfortunately discontinued, will be preferred and gone on with before other public buildings of a similar kind are initiated?

I think that is a very fair question. I feel that is the course that I should pursue as Minister of Public Works, and will certainly reoommend to my colleagues. Of course there may be other cases arise, such as a public building being burned down or a wharf being carried away, which might create an exception, and we might have to include these new works, but as a general principle I am and would be committed to
those works which parliament was asked to sanction last year.
Does that apply to breakwaters and wharfs as well as to public build-invs?
Yes. Of course, if I were convinced that any work was not necessary I would have to think the matter over, but as at present advised I would adopt that course.

I am referring to the items whioh were in the estimates last year and which are stricken out of the estimates of the present year, and which of course would not be placed in the estimates last year if the ministry did not consider they were justifiable.
Now I would like to ask the minister, because I am in receipt of many inquiries from Westport, whether he considers this public landing at Westport would be a work which, under the policy here stated, would be proceeded with next year. I may say that there is great need, and has been for many years, of a public landing at Westport. Westport is an important town where a large business is carried on, and which a laTge fleet of fishing and trading vessels frequents. It has steamboat connection with St. John, but owing to the extreme rise and fall of the tide there the people of that port and the travelling public generally, are very much incommoded from the lack of a proper landing place for vessels. In fact matters have come to such a pass that the steamer which calls from St. John is obliged to lay off in the stream at certain periods of the tide, and the only way the people can land is to wade through the water and mud to the shore, or to climb ashore bv means of lobster crates and devices of that character. I would urge upon the minister the necessity of the construction of that landing. It was promised last year and Was included in the estimates, but owing to the straightened financial condition,"he has not considered it advisable to go on with that work the present year. May I ask him if, under these circumstances, it will be one of those works to which preference will be given, and that the people in that district may look for the beginning of the work next year?

I regret that I am not able to give any assurance with regard to this work, or with regard to other works, Specifically. I have nothing to add to the statement I made upon a previous occasion. Of course if I have to determine as between different works in the estimates, I might take up some works in preference to others according to the public necessity. But it did not follow from the remarks I made that all of the works in the estimates would be taken up at the same time. Some may have to stand over. Therefore, I hope my hon. friend will not ask me to give any specific promise as to this work. He will simply have to rely upon the statement I made of a general character on a previous occasion.

It must have been recognized by the minister that there was a pressing necessity for a public landing at Westport when he included in the estimates of last year an appropriation towards its construction. Taking that as a basis and recognizing the necessity of the landing I will not ask whether it will be given preference over other works of a similar character which have been deferred, but I will ask whether it will not be given preference over new works for which there was no appropriation in last year's estimates?

I cannot give my hon. friend any assurance, because it may be that when the time comes to provide for further works some will be brought to my notice of a much more pressing character than the particular work to which he refers.

Then does the minister wish me to understand that he does not consider that this is a work which was necessary and that the appropriation which was made last year was made, not with the intention of going on with the work, but for some other purpose; or, does he believe that the work was necessary and that the appropriation of last year was honestly placed there?

The amount that was placed in the estimates last year was placed there in good faith and with the sincere belief that the works were a public necessity. I do not at all wish to withdraw a single word which I uttered in this chamber on a previous occasion with regard to this. My hon. friend must see that where some $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 have been struck off my estimates the time will soon come when parliament would feel like providing for a portion of that amount. I might have half the amount placed at my disposal and then I would have to discriminate between works which might stand over and works which were more imperative. There might also be new works which would be of the most urgent character. Under these circumstances I could not be expected in any way to bind the government or parliament as to what appropriations would be passed upon a future occasion. The very best I can do is to rely upon the statement which I made and which is fully reported in ' Hansard.' As to giving individual promises that this or that work will be undertaken, I must decline to do so. I could not with any degree of propriety give any assurance as to what action may be taken by the government at the next or any subsequent session.

The necessity for a public landing is greater and more urgent today than it was when that amount was placed in the estimates and the only changed condition, as far as Westport and the county of Digby generally is concerned, Mr. PUGSLEY.
is that a Conservative and not a Liberal is now representing that county in this parliament. I trust that that is not the reason upon which the minister is basing his remarks. I trust he will not allow a trifling matter of that sort to cause him to discriminate against Westport. Westport, has always been very faithful to Liberal traditions. Westport has always given a large Liberal majority. Westport has never had any assistance of this character from the public exchequer since 1896. Last year, when the election was imminent and when the people of Westport were beginning to be restive and suggested that they might not always support the Liberal policy, the promise was made to them that a public landing would be provided and an appropriation was placed in the estimates for its construction. Then the people of Westport did as they always have done in the past -walked up to the polls and gave a very good majority for the Liberal candidate. But the county generally did not follow their example and the Liberal canddate was unable to secure a majority in the county. But, I do not think that should be any reason why the people of Westport should be deprived of their share of the public moneys or why the minister should refrain from giving them any assurance that, so soon as the public funds will permit the construction of this work it will be proceeded with. I do not think it is unreasonable to ask the minister if he has changed his mind with regard to the necessity of the work. I think it is only right and proper, in view of the fact that this item was stricken out of the estimates and people have been told that the work will not be proceeded with now that they should be given the reason why this has been so stricken out and that they should also be given some assurance as to whether the work will be proceeded with when the public funds permit of the undertaking being carried on.
I have neither changed my mind nor have I seen any reason for changing my mind. But, as to giving any assurance, I do not feel that my hon. friend can properly ask me to do that.
How much of the $l,j 200 voted last year was spent on the Brule wharf and how much of the $1,000 voted last year was spent on the Economy wharf?

That is not in the estimates. If my hon. friend will be good enough to put a question in the House I shall be glad to answer it. The information I have here appertains to the estimates that I am asking the committee to vote.
I thought your officers would know.
They would not carry these things in their heads.

The information I have got is that none of this money has been spent. As I stated some evenings ago, I suggested the appointment of men to look after the work to be done by day's work, but my men were not taken on. Of course, I know there was an election on last year and there will probably not be another for four years.

Perhaps I am responsible that my hon. friend has not been further consulted with regard to the em-employment of the men because I really thought it would be imposing a burden on the hon. gentleman that he would not like to assume.

If I had been consulted the money would have been spent honestly, and not stolen as it had been in the past. As to the Economy wharf it is known as the camel back wharf and I took a snap shot of it, but unfortunately when I developed the plate it did not turn out very well.
Did it break the kodak?

Well not quite. The approach to the wharf runs in a semicircle so that a team can hardly drive on to it. I cannot understand why for the sake of $1,000 the wharf is left in that condition. It would seem that wherever a Conservative is elected there is no money to be spent.

I wish to direct the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the work at Naufrage pond, Prince Edward Island. At page 1347 of 'Hansard,' in reply to Mr. Ames the minister states that in the month of December the government made up their mind to drop certain public works for which tenders had been called. Further on he was asked by Mr. Foster to give a concrete instance of a public work for which tenders had been advertised but which would not be proceeded with, and the minister says:
There was the case of the Naufrage pond in Prince Edward Island. The constituency had been asking for this for a considerable time but the amount was large, and although we asked for tenders we concluded that we might allow that to stand for another year. The matter was referred to the chief engineer and he reported that he did not think the public interest would suffer if it were allowed to stand for another year.
Now, notwithstanding that statement of the minister I find at page 64 of the estimates for the coming year an item of $14,500 for protecting works at the entrance of Naufrage pond. There seems to be a discrepancy between the item in the estimates and the statement of the minister, and I would now ask him if it is the intention of the government to go ahead with the work this year?

It would be more convenient if the hon. gentleman would ask me the question when we come to that item.
Clark's harbour-protection works, $800.
What is the nature of the work at Clark's harbour?
The construction of beach protection works to protect the houses, stores and boat landings from danger of encroachment by the sea.
What has been expended previously on that?
What is the extent of these beach protection works?
926 feet long and 3 feet high.
Does it run along a roadway or along private lands ?
I do not know.

It is very material that we should know that. There is a distinction between protecting public property, private property, and government property. Will this be for the protection of government property?
It protects the property of quite a considerable number of people.
Was there a petition in favour of this work?
I think there must have been.
This item should stand until the minister can tell us whether this work is to protect the property of some private individual or whether it is to protect work along some highway.

There is no question but that it is to protect such a number of properties as to make it of an entirely public nature. It is in no sense to protect the property of a private individual in the sense my hon. friend suggests.
Well, it must either be for the protection of public property or of private property.
When you get a large number of people whose property is to be protected the protection becomes of a public nature.

I am moved to ask these questions because some time ago the department was asked to protect property which is partly owned by the government, in Digby. I refer to the property locally known as Battery Point. It was protected many years ago but the protection work

has fallen into decay and the bank has tumbled down by the erosion of the tides, and has fallen into the harbour. The town of Digby has gone to very great expense in protecting the beach and foreshore generally, but they do not feel they should protect this particular government property nor indeed are they financially able to do so. If the minister thinks a policy of protecting the property of individuals is justifiable, is it not more obviously necessary to protect the property of the government?
I think it is the duty of the government reasonably to protect its own property.
Then will the minister make a note of this so that he may make provision for the protection of this property?

I will make a note of it with pleasure.
Cow hay-Port Morien.-harbour improvements, $5,000.

How much was spent on that breakwater in the year 1908?	$18,000
was voted, and $2,500 is re-voted now.
That would leave $15,500 as our expenditure to the 31st of this month.
There would be no expenditure during the months of December, January, February and March on a breakwater at Cow bay?
I do not know that that would be the case. I should think material could be got out during that time.
In the fiscal year ending March 31, 1907, the material that was used in those months was a little hardware, some white duck and some cement.
Could they not manufacture concrete blocks in the winter?
No, they could not.
I have an impression that they could. They do.

They do manufacture concrete blocks two feet square for the purpose of erecting buildings; but they do not make concrete blocks for breakwaters of the dimensions mentioned in the report of the Minister of Public Works. These blocks are not made and then transported and dumped into the harbour. They are erected in the water at low tide, and that could not be done in the winter time. Were tenders asked for this work in 1907 or 1908?
No. The opinion of the chief engineer was that this work latterly had better be done bv day work.

Would the minister consider that the man in charge of building a breakwater of this character should be a man having a special knowledge of the building of breakwaters, the mixing of concrete and that sort of thing?
I should say he should have a thorough knowledge of it.

Is the minister aware that P. J. Leslie, who did the work in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1907, who used 2,513 barrels of sand and 1,873 barrels of cement, and who superintended the work at $3 per day, is a lobster packer, who packs his catch at Port Morien in the summer time and lives at Halifax in the winter months?
I am not aware of that.
Is the minister learning that for the first time now?
This is the first time I have heard of it.
Who recommended Mr. Leslie to the department?
The inspector is always approved of by the engineer in charge.
Who was the engineer in charge?
Mr. Millidge is, I think, the resident engineer there. .
Who was in charge during the last fiscal year ending the 31st of March of this year?
I think Mr. Leslie is still in charge, but I am not quite sure as to that.
Does the minister know as a matter of fact who was in charge during the expenditure of the sum of $15,500?
My memorandum shows that Mr. Leslie is still in charge; but if my hon. friend says that he was not, I will look it up.

Is the minister of Public Works aware that the man who succeeded Leslie and had charge of that work during the summer and up to October, 1908, was a butcher of the name of McLeod, who if building a flue or a foundation to his House, would hire a mason' Mr. PUGSLEY. I am not aware of that.
Will the minister tell me who recommended the person in charge of the work for the fiscal year 1908-09?
I am sorry to say I have no memorandum in reference to that.

In view of the fact that this breakwater is of considerable importance to Port Morien, that it was built by

the Gowrie, Blockhouse and Coal Mining Company previous to 1873, that it originally extended a distance of 1,374 feet, practically a quarter of a mile, to 17 feet at low water or to 23 feet at high water, and was about 44 feet in width; that the property was subsequently transferred to the Dominion Coal Company; that part of the breakwater was destroyed by the August gale of 1873; that the present structure is 1,114 feet long, that is, 160 feet shorter than it was when the Gowrie Blockhouse and Coal Mining Company constructed it; and in view of the development of mining areas there by their successors, the Dominion Coal Company, and the recently commenced developments of the North Atlantic Colliery Company, which would indicate that a great deal of shipping would be made from that port; in view also of the fact that $15,500 has been spent on this breakwater in 1907-08 and $11,500 in 1906-07, and that $5,000 is to be expended in the incoming year, making a total expenditure of $32,000 in three years; does it not appear to the minister that it would be wise to have this money spent by some one who understood the construction of breakwaters, under the circumstances that obtain at that particular point, where the gales have carried away from time to time considerable portions of this breakwater? The minister's own report says that in 1895 it was torn to pieces.
I suppose it was not being as well constructed then as it is now.

It has been going to pieces again in 1908, and it will continue to go to pieces so long as butchers and lobster packers dump concrete cement in canvas bags on that coast in the month of October. I submit, in view of the necessity of this breakwater, that a survey should be made and estimates obtained for the purpose of building a permanent structure. The expenditure of such large sums should be made through contractors under tender and give to that harbour a permanent structure instead of expending money in such a manner as cannot give permanent satisfaction. In 1907-08, when $11,509 were spent, that expenditure covered a period of over 180 working days during which 12 men per day on an average were working. It is common knowledge to any one familiar with that coast that in the months of April and May, with high spring tides and strong winds from the north-east, and drifting ice hanging about that part of the coast, especially in 1907, when that harbour was ice-bound until the 7th June, it must be manifest that the suspension of canvas sacks down the side of the breakwater and filling with cement is not calculated to make a permanent structure, such as a breakwater. Is it the minister's intention to have the further sum of $5,000 spent by some butcher or lobster packer or by someone who has some knowledge of the work the government purposes to undertake?
Does the hon. gentleman give me the assurance that the inspector is not a practical man in concrete work ?

I would say that Mr. Leslie is not a competent man to undertake the repairs of a breakwater of this kind. He has no experience either in stone work or concrete, and the man who suc-ceded him is if anything more incompetent than Mr. Leslie, not having had the experience at the expense of the government which Mr. Leslie had.

I am glad the matter has been brought to my notice. I shall have inquiry made to ascertain if the inspector is not a practical man having practical knowledge of concrete work. _ It is important he should be, because it is work which depends greatly on the quality of the cement used and the mode of mixing it.
I shall have inquiries made at once, and if I find that the inspector is not a practical man, I shall see that one is put on the works. The instructions given to the resident engineer are always to find out whether the man suggested as inspector is a practical man.
What are his political affiliations?
That does not concern me.
Is the same letter issued to the resident engineers in Nova Scotia as is issued to those in Quebec, instructing them to apply to the local member for foremen of their various works?
The same letter.
The department sends a letter from Ottawa to the local resident engineer telling him to appoint no foremen except on consultation with the local Liberal member.

I do not think these are the terms of the letter, but if my hon. friend has it he can correct me. What is done is that the resident engineer is instructed to confer with the member as to the employment of the foreman, but his positive instructions are not to engage any man in special work of this nature unless he is a practical man and has practical knowledge.
Would the minister produce a copy of the letter sent by the department so that we may have it on record?
If there is a motion made in the regular way the letter will be brought down.
Is. it not the rule of the House that if a minister refers to a document he must produce it?
The reference was made by the hon. member for St. Antoine. What I said was that any letters sent out to the other provinces were not different from the ones sent to Quebec.
Adverting again to Mr. Leslie at Cow Bay, in view of the fact that the lobster season begins in the latter part of March and continues to June.
Is the hon. gentleman opposed to the item passing?
Certainly not.
Then it might be as well for him not to obstruct it.

I am not opposed to the expenditure. If I have any fault to find it is that the break-water is inadequate. What I am opposed to is the system of expenditure. We could have a better break-water there if the money had been judiciously expended. In view of the fact that the lobster packing begins in the spring, is it proper that Mr. Leslie should draw $3 a day for inspecting the work on the breakwater when he is at the same time superintending the packing of lobsters when he employs a large number of people. In other words, does the Minister of Public Works think it advisable to encourage a man like Mr. Leslie to try to serve two masters?
I think that, if he is appointed inspector he should be there.

I do not think there is any desire on the part of anybody who knows this work to obstruct the expenditure. I know Mr. Leslie, the gentleman who has been referred to, to be a decent, respectable man. I know that he does not live in this place, but he lives in part of the Sutv Bay and Port Halifax and Halifax City.
Where does he live in the summer ?

For a few months in the summer, he is in Cow Bay packing lobsters as the _ minister has been informed. I should judge from the information that we get from the minister that he did not know much about Mr. Leslie, but he is bound to make inquiry and to remove any wrong.
1 he expenditure on this breakwater is one that is required; I know the locality well, and I know that this is an important work. But the minister, I am sure, will not complain when we try to give him. information that will assist in the best expenditure of this money, because we wish the money to be spent to the best advantage, as I am sure the minister does also. If, even at this late date, he finds that the man in charge
of the work should not be in charge
What does the hon. member (Mr. Crosby) think of Mr. Leslie?
I have said he is a decent, respectable man, and a good citizen. If he has a fault, it is that he is a strong Liberal.

Does the hon. gentleman think that Mr. Leslie is competent for this
work ?
I think he knows no more about concrete work than does the hon. gentleman who is now addressing the committee-'and that is not much.

I will look into it at
once.
The minister should see to it that proper men are put in charge of the work.

I think the point raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Mad-din) is a very important one. A great deal of money is expended on operations done by day's work under the Public Works Department, and it is to be expected and desired that the persons in charge of these works should be compentent men, selected by the engineer without outside interference, and purely because they are able men for the work. In our province, there has been a system of applying to the local member, not for advice, but for the absolute choice of the man who shall be placed in charge of each of these works. Here is a letter, dated May 4, and addressed to Mr. J. c! Tache, resident engineer of the Department of Public Works at Chicoutimi, and the question I was putting to the minister a few moments ago is whether a similar letter is sent to the resident engineers throughout Nova Scotia, and whether a similar system is adopted in the choice of a foreman to overlook day's work in that province. This letter is written by the chief engineer at Ottawa to the resident engineer at Chicoutimi :	,
I am directed by the hon. the minister to authorize you to proceed, by day labour, with the works at the following places, for which appropriations have been granted by parliament during the session just ended. Will you please apply to the persons mentioned for the names of competent foremen, or for any other information which you may require in connection with the works in their respective counties.
And the name given here is that of Joseph Girard, M.P., for Chicoutimi and Saguenay. The letter proceeds :
You will please bear in mind that the above-mentioned sum must on no account be over-expended, and I would ask you to give positive instructions to the foremen to that effect. The foremen are to be paid at the rate of $2.50 per day, unless you are otherwise instructed.
There is absolutely nothing in that letter from the chief engineer, acting under

the minister, demanding that the resident engineer shall choose competent men and men who have knowledge of the work under their charge. The only thing he is told to do is to apply to the local member and put on the job whomsoever he recommends.
It says ' competent foremen.'
But the judging of their competency is left to the local member.
By no means.
Is it under this system that the lobster packer and butcher have been chosen to superintend the work at Cow Bay, where we are spending from $10,000 to $15,000 a year ?

I would point out that my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) is hardly fair or candid in dealing with this subject when he attempts to misconstrue the letter to which he has referred so as to lead the committee to believe that it did not rest with the engineer to determine the competency of the men who might be recommended by Mr. Girard. The ordinary rules of grammatical interpretation of any document must show us that the letter calls for competent men who may be recommended by Mr. Girard, and that as to their competency, .the resident engineer himself is to determine. And the minister informs me that there were special instructions besides. The engineer was asked to secure, on Mr. Girard's nomination, competent men. That could not be determined by a member of parliament but was to' be determined by the engineer responsible for the work. The naming of the man would be for the member, but the judging of his competency would be for the engineer. I do not think that the hon. member (Mr. Ames) is so innocent as not to know that this system of getting members of parliament to recommend men who might be employed in matters of this kind has been going on since confederation. It is no great discovery to make in this forty-second year of confederation that men are recommended for employment by members supporting the government. Is there anything new, or anything very wrong about it?
' By their fruits ye shall know them.' And what kind of men do we get?

As good men, and in many cases better than those the country had when my hon. friend's friends were in power. Who are the best judges of these men unless it be the representative of the county? And who knows the men better than the man who represents the county?
That is Mr. Maddin.
Apparently, he does not want it, and besides he is not in the confidence of the government.
The hon. gentleman said ' representative.'

In this case I was discussing what my hon. friend from St. Antoine had said with regard to Chicoutimi and Mr. Girard, and was dealing with this case as one illustrating the general principle. The question of recommending to the government a man to have charge of an expenditure is not a question of competency only. A map. might be competent but not honest; he might not want the government instructions to be carried out, and certainly the government would not want to be responsible for a man who is not recommended by one in whom they have confidence. Is this a new doctrine? Why do these hon. gentlemen prate about a thing that their friends did when they were in power, and would do again if they came into power to-morrow? We might as well be frank about this. No government would accept the recommendation of a man who did not have their confidence. Only yesterday, my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) started a discussion which took the whole afternoon about an expenditure in Nova Scotia. But if the Conservative candidate in that riding had been elected and sat here as a representative even if he had not recommended the man in charge, they would not have raised any question about that expenditure. If recommendations of the men who are to be inspectors were left in the hands of the opponents of the government, what a nice time hon. gentlemen opposite would have criticising the Minister of Public Works.
I should be sorry to believe that the ideals which the member for Pic-tou (Mr. Macdonald) says are shared by all, are likely to be the ideals which are forever to obtain in this country.

Is my hon. friend any better than his party, when he is claiming high ideals? Any better than Sir John Thompson, or Sir John A. Macdonald, who led his party before him, and who instituted that system?

I would think that the practice the Minister of Public Works should adopt would be for his chief engineer to secure, in the first place, a competent resident engineer, and then let him choose the most competent man to be found in the neighbourhood as inspector of the construction of the public work. Then I think we would get honest work done, work that was worth 100 cents on the dollar.

We are here discussing a question of expenditure, because we have

reason to believe that there has been waste in connection with it. I know this Mr. Leslie, he is a councillor in the municipality of Halifax. I do not know whether he understands the kind of concrete that should be used in this breakwater, but he may understand some other kind of concrete he gets from the government. He is not a man I would select to superintend the building of a concrete work. In the county of Cape Breton there must be somebody that knows just as much about concrete work as Mr. Leslie; therefore it is strange that he should be appointed to a position of that kind, when he is not a resident of the county, does not live near the county at all, but only visits there during the lobster season, which lasts only about six weeks in the summer. I would have no objection to the appointment of a Liberal if he was suitable for the work.
The minister has not a.nswer-ed my question as to whether a similar letter is issued to his officials in Nova Scotia?
I have not seen any letter issued in Nova Scotia, but I have no doubt similar instructions are given to the resident engineers.
The member for Pictou has intimated that there are other instructions which go with it.

We are in touch with the resident engineers all the time, and they understand that it is their duty not to accept as inspector any man who in their judgment is not thoroughly competent to inspect the work.
I understood the minister to say that written instructions accompany the letter.
They have their general instructions, they understand that in no case shall they accept an inspector who is not thoroughly competent.
Then will the minister lay on the table to-morrow any letter of this character which is issued to resident engineers in Nova Scotia, together with any other instructions which may accompany the same?
Yes, to-morrow, or at an early date, if there are such.
Can the minister mention an instance where the resident engineer has declined to accept the nominee of the party?'
Not at the moment, but I know it has happened.

There are a number of constituencies in Nova Scotia that are not represented by members supporting the government. I would like to know upon whose recommendation, in those eonstitu-Mr. CROSBY.
encies, the resident engineer appoints an inspector?
The instructions in that case were to confer with the gentleman who had run in the interest of the government. That is the course which has always been pursued.

In view of this statement by the minister, it is a question whether we should proceed any further with the consideration of this vote. It seems to me a shocking statement for a responsible minister to make to this parliament, that the government should adopt so low an ideal, that they should place in the hands of a defeated candidate the appointing power, no matter how small may be the number of electors who voted for him, and no matter what his standing in the community may be.
What would the hon. gentleman say if he was defeated by a bogus telegram?
I was saying when the hon. gentleman so rudely interrupted me

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not in order to attribute rudeness to an hon. member.

The Chairman reminds me that it is not in order to describe the remark of the hon. member, but I would like to say that it is much more an offence for any hon. gentleman to be rude to a member who is addressing the House than it is for the member who is on his feet to express his view of the interruption. But, since the falsifying of a telegram is introduced into this discussion I would like to ask the hon. gentleman who has interrupted me why he does not first pay attention to his own household, why he does not first have an investigation into his own Department of Justice which is much closer to him than the location of the despatch to which he has alluded.
I would like to call his attention to the
Do you not think, Mr Chairman, that instead of discussing William Miner we might take up this item?

-falsification of the telegram addressed to the Department of Justice and ask if these hon. gentlemen have taken any precaution to investigate that. I say that until they do take that precaution it ill becomes them to refer to any other despatch of that nature. Apologizing for this digression, made in answer to the unseemly interruption of the hon. gentleman, I would like to return to the subject which brought me to my feet and say that I do not think we should subscribe to the extraordinary doctrine laid down by the Minister of Public Works that he should

accept the advice of persons outside of this parliament, who have been rejected by the electors of any constituency, who have been turned down and whose places have been taken by the men who sit in this House. We should not subscribe to the doctrine enunciated by the minister that he should take their advice in preference to ours. That is a doctrine which is offensive to the dignity of this House, one to which this House should not assent, and the fact that it has been laid down by the Minister of Public Works on this occasion is a sufficient ground for us to declare a halt in these proceedings and ask for the adjournment of this committee so that we may take into consideration whether or not the parliament of Canada subscribes to a standard so low.

We all recall the words of the minister earlier m the session when he stated that the patronage list had been entirely abolished. Has the minister issued fresh instructions since then to the responsible engineers asking them to discontinue the old system of making appointments and to select only the best men.

There has been no change in the instructions which have gone to the engineers as to the appointment of foremen and the selection of their men.
Cow Bay Run and Osbornes-breakwaters,

This is a revote to complete the work.
Cribbin's Point wharf-part renewal of superstructure, $3,300.

This is a revote to complete the repairs.
Digby harbour -* improvements, including repairs and additions to pier, $30,000.
This is under contract.
Who has the contract?
Messrs. G. E. and A. Bigelow.
What are the terms of the contract?
The date of the contract is the 22nd of May, 1908, and the date of completion is the 22nd of November, 1909.
What will be the rate of remuneration?
The foreman on the works according to my memorandum is to get $2.50 per day.
What is the amount of the contract?
$17,900. This will construct the spur pier. It does not include the taking down of the old pier and rebuilding it with creosoted timber.
Does this include anything for the reconstruction of the old work?

We will require about $30,000 more to finish up the whole work.
Harbours and rivers, Nova Scotia-harbours, rivers and bridges-general repairs and improvements, $30,000.
This is a general vote.
Is there anything included in this for the construction of a wharf at Spry bay, Halifax county? Was it not commenced last year?
Yes, we spent $269 last year and if any small amount is required we can take it out of the general vote for this year.
The work that was done there was very small and in order to make it of any service it will be necessary to have some further work done there this year.
No doubt that will be considered by the engineers.

There is a wharf in Halifax county at Peswick near Musquodo-boit. There was a wharf constructed at the head of the harbour. While it serves a good purpose there it would have been of greater service if it had been constructed nearer the mouth of the harbour on the west side. There should be a further expenditure of $1,000 to build a block for the use of the fishermen at the mouth of the harbour. I would like to bring that to the notice of the minister and I would be glad if he would ask his engineers to make some inquiry about it.
I will have an inquiry made.
Will the minister explain the reason for inserting the word 'bridges' in this item ?
That has no application to Nova Scotia but it is a general term used in reference to the other provinces where there may be inter-provincial bridges.
It might apply to the bridge the minister built at Tatamagouche Bay about a year ago.
That was a wharf.
The photograph shows it is a bridge.
The province built the bridge.
Well, it has dropped down about 18 inches and is in need of repair.
That is worthy of attention.

I wish to refer to the Sandy Cove breakwater which was built by the government in 1904. The minister, in reply to questions put to him this session stated that the contractors for this breakwater were released and their deposit of $800 returned to them on the 3rd of December, 1904. Subsequent to that the department received notice that a number of labourers on that work were unpaid and that certain men who had furnished material which had gone into its construction also remained unpaid. This woVk was constructed at Sandy Cove on Digby Neck which there is about one mile in width. There are properly speaking two coves, one on the bay of Fundy side and one on St. Mary's bay side, and the village of Sandy Cove is located
To which item is the hon. gentleman speaking ?
I am speaking on the item before the committee.

I do not wish to interfere with the hon. gentleman discussing a question of this kind but it certainly does not arise on the vote now before the House. Let me say that this claim which the hon. gentleman is referring to has already been pressed upon the attention of the government just as strong as the hon. gentleman can press it. It has been pressed on the government by his predecessor and by the hon. member for Antigonish and the matter is now under consideration. There is nothing which my hon. friend can say to-night which can affect the determination of the question.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Jameson) is perfectly in order in speaking as he does on this item.
This is a claim against the government which if granted would be a matter of grace on the part of the department and which would require a special appropriation.
I will ask the Chairman if I am in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I was not following very closely the remarks of the hon. gentleman but on an item such as this I think it would be quite competent to refer to a vote which the hon. gentleman would desire to have in the estimates. I would not be prepared to rule that out of order.
This work is not paid out of this general vote. There was a special appropriation for it and the claim referred to by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Jameson) is in no way pertinent to this item.
I will continue what I was saying when the minister interrupted me.
What is your ruling, Mr. Chairman, in view of my statement?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If it is a matter which is under the consideration of the government in an official way it might be as well for the hon. gentleman not to press it. As there are special circumstances in connection with it a long discussion on this item would not appear to be in order.

The minister stated in reply to a question of mine that these claims had been received by the government on the 20th June, 1905, and as they have been so long under consideration I think it is mv duty to refresh the memory of the minister with regard to them. As I was saying when interrupted, this wharf was unfortunately located on the Bay of Fundy shore and not at the village of Sandy Cove proper. The construction of the work involved an expenditure larger than the contractors had estimated, and it appears they were unable to meet the cost of construction out of the money they received from 'the government. I shall not now speak in regard to the large claim of Mr. J. D. Kirk for $2,085.50 but I shall specially deal with the claims of a number of poor men, residents of that locality, for labour performed and material supplied. They supplied the labour and the material in good faith expecting to get paid for it, but their pay was not forthcoming and the government released the contractors and returned to them their deposit of $800. The government has taken over the work, and while I believe that the expenditure was not justified because of the location, as it should have been constructed on the St. Mary'* Bay side of Digby Neck and at the village of Sandy Cove, where it would have been of considerable usefulness and would have assisted in the building up of that village, yet at the same time I do believe that the men who performed this labour and supplied the material should be paid. The government has taken over the work and has the advantage of the time and labour and material supplied by the men who have made the claims. If the work was justified, as it must have been in the opinion of the department before the expenditure was made, then these men have a very strong claim on the government for the amount still due them. I am not asking that anything be done for the contractors ; I am not asking that anything be done for any one except the poor men who performed the labour and supplied the timber. I do think that their claim should be considered by the government and that payment to them should not be any longer deferred.
In justice to the residents of a certain district of my county, I desire

to bring to the minister's attention the fact that a portion of an item of $5,000 which was in the estimates last year was, I believe, expended on the construction of a wharf at Joggin's Mines. I have been advised that, owing to the work having been stopped last season and fenders not having been placed on the sides of the wharf, the work thus far done is likely to go for naught. I feel it my duty to bring the matter to the attention of the minister in the interest of public property.

I will have it looked into.
Little Narrows wharf, $1,200.
Is this a repair to an existing wharf?
No, it is for the construction of a small wharf.
Is it to be built of creo-soted timber?
We have no detailed plan yet.
I understand that the water there is largely populated by the teredo, the worm that destroys timber.

If we find on the report of the engineer that it is necessary, we will have it creosoted.
Middle river-shear dams, $700.
That is a revote.

I know that it is a revote, but it never should have been voted in the first place. As I understand it, when voting for the harbours and rivers of Nova Scotia, the term rivers means navigable rivers, for the purpose of assisting shipping. There is a small stream in Cape Breton, a trout stream which I have fished in on more than one occasion, which contains so little water in summer time that one can wade across it without getting wet above his ankles; but sometimes, when the water is high, the farm land is washed into this brook, and the department has been persuaded somehow or other that it is a part of the duty of the federal authorities to build shear dams along the banks of this small river eleven miles inland. I can imagine no excuse that can be urged that can bring that expenditure properly under the vote we are being asked for. While I do not wish to divide the House to-night, I wish to go on record as protesting against that expenditure as being wholly and completely outside of our domain. If that principle were carried out generally, and every little river in any province where there was danger of farm land being washed away by the spring freshets, was to have cribwork built along its banks by the Dominion government, and the farmers whose land was protected were paid $2.50 a
day for building it, the department would see no end to the demands that would be made upon it. In these days of economy, when we want to spend our money as carefully as possible, it seems to me that the minister should avoid expenditures of this character, which have no other than a political end.
This is a class of work which has been done more or less by all governments since confederation.
Can the minister cite any instance?

Oh, yes. In the province of New Brunswick, on the upper waters of the St. John river, ever since confederation, a few hundred dollars have been expended each year for the purpose of blasting out rocks.
That is because it is an international river.

Not at that point. Then, in the province of British Columbia work has been done, at the joint expense of the federal and provincial governments, on the Fraser and other rivers for the protection of the banks.
The Fraser is a navigable river.

The work has not been for the benefit of navigation, but for the protection of the property of the people living along the banks. In the same way twenty years ago work was done on the South Nation river, not to improve navigation, but for the purpose of enabling the water to flow more rapidly, and so preventing the lands being flooded. In the province of Nova Scotia and also in Quebec and Ontario, protection works of the same kind have been carried on. It has been done to a certain extent by both governments. Last session parliament made an appropriation to cut a channel across a portion of land near Portage la Prairie, the effect of which, it is asserted, will be to prevent the flooding of some 40,000 acres. Therefore, it is a question of degree. I admit very frankly that if this work were new, I would not at this moment and in the state of the revenues ask parliament for an appropriation; but the small amount now being asked is to complete the work which has already been begun.

There is only this to be said, that the rivers the minister has cited are all rivers in point of fact; and while what he describes may not be defensible, the crime is not so great as it is in this particular case. There is no reason why the land of the particular men on this little stream, several miles inland, should I be protected any more than that of others,

but they had some strong pull. There are. I venture to say, in Nova Scotia, 500 streams as to which a similar excuse could be urged, and if we once commence spending moneys for this purpose, there will be no end to the demands and no possibility of refusing any.

As the minister has enunciated the policy of the government on this matter, I would like to call his attention to the fact that there is a very large stream running through the country I represent, the Nottawasaga river, which is navigable for about thirty miles, and has been used for many years as a means of transportation to the north. This river overflows every spring and renders useless some 30,000 acres of most valuable land in that section. In the province of Ontario we have not been accustomed to receive many of those favours. People have to go down into their own pockets to pay for these works, and in this case those interested have not seen fit to carry on the work for many years, but last session the Ontario government gave something towards cutting that river wider and deepening it so as to protect this land.
It is undoubtedly proper provincial work.

CURRIE In the province of Ontario these works are provincial works, but not in the other provinces. I would ask the minister to bear this in mind as possibly his department may be asked to assist in that work along that river. If so, I trust he will give it the same consideration that he does these small trout streams in Nova Scotia and Cape Breton.
Minasville wharf at Dalrymple Point, $9,000.

This is for the construction of a breakwater, 300 feet long, 16 feet wide at the top, 4 feet deep at the shore and 19 feet at the outer end. Quite a number of vessels come there for lumber as well as fishing boats.
Was this under contract?

Yes, six tenders were received and the contract was let to Bigelow and Co., for $7,985. This will complete the work.
Port Hastings wharf, $11,600.

Tenders were called for and a contract entered into with W. J. Landrey, of Antigonish. This will complete the work.
Portuguese Cove breakwater-to complete payments to contractors Reid & Archibald on final estimates inclusive of interest accrued at 5 per cent per annum on overdue balance of $1,120-revote of lapsed amount, $1,100.

This is a very important work, and I would bring to the notice of the minister the necessity of having a construction at the end of the breakwater, a kind of tee. This is necessary to make it complete.

I will consider this
suggestion.
Why is 5 per cent interest to be paid to the contractor?
This is a delayed payment.
What amount is the interest?
South Lake Lakevale-opening channel from Lake St. George's bay, inclusive of protection work, $6,500.
I move to reduce that item by $4,500. The amount will be provided for in the supplementary estimates of the current year.
That is, $4,500 will be asked foi that will be spent in the year 1908-9?
Yes.
What is it required for?
For the work of opening the channel.
Has the $4,500 already been spent?
It will be spent before the end of the current year.
Is it all, or practically all, owing in wages at the present time?
Yes, practically.
Has it been owing since last September, October and November?

I cannot give the particulars. There was a mistake-I do not know whether the fault of the resident engineer or the printer-and there was delay in making provision for it, and we understood that by leaving the whole amount in the estimates of the coming year, it would delay payment, and so we intend to ask for $4,500 in the supplementaries of the current year.

Last year the amount asked was $5,625. But the Minister of Finance said:
That estimate was made some time ago. Progress has been made so that so large an amount is not required. I propose to reduce the item to $700 and move that the amount be reduced accordingly.
So, we were given to understand that $700 would be all that would be required, but in addition, $4,500 has been spent. Who made the mistake?
It was reduced through ar. error. There is a good deal of correspondence, and the matter has taken a good deal of trouble to straighten out. It was a mistake to have the vote reduced last year.

It was a mistake. In this way, if I am rightly informed: the work was commenced and was continued until the appropriation was exhausted. Legally, no more money could be expended at that point. But the elections were close at hand, and Antigonish was a close county, and the member for the county felt that it would not be well to have the work stop suddenly in September or October. So the work was continued; the men were hired but not paid, and they continued to work until some time after the election. The form of irregularity may have been avoided by not paying out money, still, the amount of $4,500 wages is due to these men for the last four or five months. That is my information.
Quite right.
Is that the principle followed in the department-that if a fund is exhausted, the department feels justified in keeping men at work trusting to a subsequent parliament to see that they are paid?
The moment an appropriation is exhausted, or even when it is about exhausted, instructions go from the chief engineer to the resident engineer to stop the work.
Why not in this case?

The amount required for this work was placed in the printed estimates which were passed by the committee, and went to the chief engineer and he gave his instructions to the resident engineer, not being aware that on concurrence the amount was reduced. But that reduction was made in error. Ordinarily, when an appropriation is about exhausted, the chief engineer sends out word to the resident engineer and the work is stopped. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Ames) will remember that in the very letter he quoted the instructions to the resident engineer were that the amounts voted must not be over expended.

But the hon. gentleman does not touch the real point. It is hardly credible that the season would have nearly slipped by before the engineer found that only $700 had been voted. That must have been discovered with the first pay -roll that came up exceeding the $700. Yet other pay-rolls came up week after week and month after month, and these were not repudiated. A search of the files of correspondence with the local men would show why the work was not stopped. We are
justified in protesting against this as an absolute irregularity. When the appropriation was exhausted, the department instead of discharging the men and taking the risk of losing the county-
The hon. member is entirely in error.

This opens up a method of doing business under stress of political pressure which shakes considerably the confidence of the people in the department. We have supposed, here in parliament, that when an appropriation for one of these works is exhausted, the work shall cease. It is a principle that has been fought for for hundreds of years that money that is not voted cannot be spent. When the appropriation was exhausted, the government should not have continued the work, even at the strenuous request of the hon. member for Antigonish to employ the men on that wharf. Is this the only case the minister knows of arising in the months of October or November?

I am sorry to see the hon. gentleman so suspicious; one so good should be disposed to be charitable. The hon. gentleman jumps at the conclusion that what was done was done at the instance of the local men.
Will the hon. minister say that there are no letters on file to that effect?	[DOT]

This was brought to my notice, and, so far as I know, no communication of any kind took place with the local men. The correspondence arose between the chief engineer of the department and the resident engineer. As I have stated, the amount was voted, and, on the strength of that the timber was procured and the work commenced. But owing to a misunderstanding, the amount was reduced on concurrence. Now at that time the work had been commenced, the timber had been bought. The deputy minister brought the matter to my notice, and I made inquiry and found a report from the resident engineer stating that unless the work was carried to completion, what was done would be absolutely destroyed and the money wasted. Under these circumstances I authorized the engineer to allow the resident engineer to go on. I thought the proper thing to do was to finish up the work.

When the minister gave that authority, did he expect that the men would be paid as they did their work ? Were the men given to understand as they worked through September, October and November, that the appropriation was exhausted, and that they would not get their money until

parliament had met and voted another appropriation ? Was it just to the men to keep them at work on the expectation that money was coming from Ottawa when no money had been voted?
The engineer was told to inform the men they would have to wait for their pay.
Did the engineer inform the men while they were still at work during those three months, that they would have to wait till parliament voted more money ?
He was instructed to do so, and I presume he did.
Would the minister lay on the table all the papers he has in connection with this transaction, within the next few days?
I will do so.
Was the minister within his right in ordering this work to go on when only $700 had been voted ? Was the minister within his right in ordering the expenditure of $7,000 more ?

I have explained that this work was done in order to prevent the loss of materials and the destruction of work ^ already done. Something similar to that is done always when a contract is let. Parliament may vote $5,000 or $10,000 for carrying on a work, which may ultimately cost three times that. But the contract is entered into subject always to parliament appropriating the necessary amounts. The contractor goes on, but of course he has to trust to (parliament making the necessary appropriation later.
Have these men been paid from any other fund, or any other source, or is the money due to these men personally ?
I do not know whether the men have been paid yet or not. I could find out. I will undertake to get that information.
I would like to ask the minister a question. Supposing there had not been an election last year, would these men have been paid ? Would they have been kept on the work ?
Everything would have been done exactly as it has been done.
This looks like an election job.
No, the election had nothing to do with it.
I understand the minister will give us all the papers in connection with this matter, with all the letters from the local members with reference to it.

I will be glad to do so. Mr. AMES.
Tangier harbour-wharf extension, $1,000.
That is in Halifax county, and is to extend the wall which was built in 1907-8. This will complete the work, which is being done by clay's labour. We have only obtained the material.

When did you obtain the
material ?

The expenditure up to the 1st of January was only $328, evidently for material.
Wallace bridge-wharf, $1,000.
This is to complete the construction of a wharf at Wallace bridge. The wharf runs at right angles with the bridge, towards the harbour.

With respect to the wharf at Wallace bridge, I put a question on the Order Paper the other day, and the minister stated in answer that the total cost was $1,324, and that a portion of it was completed. Is there another portion of this wharf to be completed, and is this vote to complete that other portion ?
The total cost was estimated at $2,500. We had an appropriation last year of $1,500, that leaves a balance of $1,000.

In the reply the minister
gave to me he said that a portion was completed, and that small vessels could use it.
We are not asking now any vote for an extension. This finishes the work.

Then this vote does not agree with the answers the_ minister gave
me.
Evidently there was an application for a further extension which we have not decided to make.
Has any portion of this $1,000 been expended?
No portion of this has been expended. This will complete the required work.

Is the minister quite certain that none of that money has been
expended?

No, none.
Yarmouth harbour-improvements, $60,000.
This is to continue the dredging work there.
Is it under contract?
Yes, to the Dominion Dredging Company.
What rate per yard?
Fifty cents per cubic yard.
To what depth?
To a depth suitable for those large steamers plying between Boston and Yarmouth.
Is it to straighten the harbour ?
Yes.
Will this complete the proposed improvements ?
No, you can dredge a long time before you finish. As you keep diedging, the boats are getting larger.
Have this Dominion Dredging Company their own dredges ?
Yes, they have quite a large fleet of dredges in different parts of Canada.
Who is at the head of this company ?
I think it is Mr. Stewart.
Of Ottawa?
Yes.
The son of the exmember ?
Yes.
May I ask the minister if this 50 cents per cubic yard means scow measurement ?	.
Yes, scow measurement.
Is it the policy of the government to favour dredging by scow measurement all over the country ?
I do not know about it being the policy of the department, but that is the way it is being done.

I would like to know why a different policy is being pursued by the Department of Railways and Canals and the Department of Public Works? When the Department of Railways and Canals let their dredging contracts it is always in situ and when the Department of Public Works let their contracts it is always scow measurement. When we get evidence before the Public Accounts Committee from officials of the Department of Railways and Canals they say that the only way that the government are safe in letting these contracts is to provide for measurement in situ. When we get the engineers of the Department of Public Works before that committee they say that scow measurement is the only safe
way as far as keeping tally upon the work is concerned. I would like to know why there should be this difference in policy between these two departments?

In the case of canal work there is no difficulty at all in taking measurements in situ by cross sections and soundings. By reason of the work being confined to narrow dimensions measurement in situ can very easily be made. In the case of harbour works it is more difficult to make measurements with- sufficient accuracy to make sure that you can determine the quantity to be dredged by measurements in situ. Of course, if you can rely upon the honesty and carefulness of your inspectors I would think that scow measurement would be more accurate. Everything depends on the integrity and carefulness of the inspectors. Canal dredging would be something like dredging for crib sites. In the case of dredging for crib sites at Quebec hon. gentlemen will remember that the tender was for measurement in situ, but in ordinary harbour work where it is not confined to narrow dimensions, I should think that scow measurement would be the more accurate provided the inspectors could be relied upon.

As far as the Department of Railways and Canals are concerned I do not think the minister will pretend that their work is entirely canal work. I know of a case in my own county where there was no canal work about it at all; it was simply dredging, widening and deepening the river between Prescott ana the next village. It was similar to harbour work and in that case it was measured in situ. As far as the inspectors are concerned, I think it was proved in the Public Accounts that, as a general rule, the inspectors who are appointed are not men of experience. We had a case last year before the Public Accounts Committee m which a shoemaker was appointed.
I do not think that was so The late member for Simcoe had a strong idea of that kind but it was not shared in by many.

I think the minister will agree that the inspector we had before the public accounts Committee last year was a man not qualified for the position. In that case there was an inspector appointed for two dredges working a mile apart.
The best qualification fcr an inspector is to be thoroughly honest.
There were two inspectors appointed, but one did the work and had a rake off from the other.
I think that only lasted a very short time. The man was dismissed.
No, the work was finished.
The work was not finished, but he was refused employment next year.
I dare say.
From what I have seen of scow measurement I do not think there is any doubt but that in every case the government are defrauded.
I hardly think that. We are extremely careful.

No matter how honest the ministers and his officers may be it cannot be avoided. I have seen work going on in my county and I have no confidence whatever in scow measurement. If an in situ contract is let I believe the work will be carried out in an honest way but I have no confidence in so far as scow measurement is concerned. I believe the Department of Public Works are paying an enormous amount for work more than is being paid by, any other department that lets contracts by the in situ method.

Take the western entrance to Toronto harbour; the measurement there is in situ. To do dredging work all over the country where it is not confined within narrow limits, it would require a very large and extensive staff of engineers. It would all have to be sounded with the very greatest care. Then, as to the different materials there would have to be a very careful examination beforehand. I am not thoroughly wedded to the scow measurement; it is a question for consideration.

The best evidence I have had of this is what the contractors themselves tell me. Contractors who have been doing work for the government for years have told me that if they could get a contract from the Department of Public Works on the principle of scow measurement they could take it at almost any price and make money out of it.
Who in the world ever tcld you that?
A contractor working for the Public Works Department.
Would you mind giving me his name?
I do not think it would be fair to the contractor, but if I gave his name he would never get a contract in the Public Works Department again.
Perhaps he is a gentleman who never did get a contract.
He is working to-day for the Public Works Department.
And if he does that it shows the man is a scoundrel.
It does not.
It does. It shows he conspires with the inspectors to defraud the government and I should be sorry either to take that man's word or to give him a contract under the government.

I do not agree witji the minister, for the reason that the department lets the contract, scow measurement. If it is in situ there is not any possible chance of his getting any more than he would be entitled to, but with the scow measurement the inspector simply passes it along. We had evidence in the committee that there are from 20 yards to 40 yards difference in each scow; that a scow would hold 100 yards when there might be only 80 yards in it.

Does not the hon. gentleman know that the quantities must be certified to by the contractor's own man as well as by the inspector for the government. There is no way of defrauding the government unless the contractor is guilty of conspiracy jointly with the inspector.
The contractor has nothing to do with it.
Yes he has.
The government inspector is responsible for the certificate.
Does the hon. gentleman think the inspector would be dishonest unless the contractor offers him some inducement to be so?
It was proved before the Public Accounts Committee last year that some of these inspectors were dishonest.
Without being induced by the contractor to be dishonest?
Yes.
Then what possible object could the inspector have in being dishonest ?
It was proved that one inspector was not attending to two different works.
That man was dismissed.
It was proved the contractors were getting more than they were entitled to.
Does the hon. gentleman say that an inspector would he dishonest without connivance with the contractor?
The contractor would not have anything to do with it.
Do you think a man would be deliberately dishonest without any one wanting him to be dishonest?
Who is the inspector and what is the amount of the contract?
$5 per cubic yard for rock, and 50 cents and 35 cents for other material.
What is the name of the inspector?

The inspectors are Messrs. Johnston, Crosby and Kimball.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Supply: Public Works, and as we will likely go through them very quickly we will take up Interior and Marine afterwards, and probably Mines later on in the day.
Will you take the Public Works for Prince Edward Island and Quebec as the first order ?

I think they will be the first.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 1.45 a.m. Friday.

Friday, March 12, 1909.
